questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q:
If the system of linear equations:
$x+y+z=6$,
$x+2y+5z=10$,
$2x+3y+\lambda z=\mu$
has infinitely many solutions, then the value of $\lambda+\mu$ equals:
questions.solution:
For the system of linear equations to have infinitely many solutions, the determinant of the coefficient matrix $\Delta$ must be zero, and $\Delta_x = \Delta_y = \Delta_z = 0$.

$\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 5 \\ 2 & 3 & \lambda \end{vmatrix} = 0$

Expanding the determinant:

$1(2\lambda - 15) - 1(\lambda - 10) + 1(3 - 4) = 0$

$\lambda - 6 = 0 \Rightarrow \lambda = 6$

Now, setting $\Delta_z = 0$:

$\Delta_z = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 1 & 2 & 10 \\ 2 & 3 & \mu \end{vmatrix} = 0$

Expanding the determinant:

$1(2\mu - 30) - 1(\mu - 20) + 6(3 - 4) = 0$

$\mu - 16 = 0 \Rightarrow \mu = 16$

Therefore, $\lambda + \mu = 6 + 16 = 22$.

Answer: $22$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q:
The sum of all possible values of $\theta \in [0, 2\pi]$, for which the system of equations :
$x\cos 3\theta - 8y - 12z = 0$
$x\cos 2\theta + 3y + 3z = 0$
$x + y + 3z = 0$
has a non-trivial solution, is equal to :
questions.solution:
For the given system of homogeneous linear equations to have a non-trivial solution, the determinant of the coefficient matrix must be zero.

$\begin{vmatrix} \cos 3\theta & -8 & -12 \\ \cos 2\theta & 3 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 & 3 \end{vmatrix} = 0$

Expanding the determinant along the first row:

$\cos 3\theta (9 - 3) - (-8)(3\cos 2\theta - 3) + (-12)(\cos 2\theta - 3) = 0$

$6\cos 3\theta + 24\cos 2\theta - 24 - 12\cos 2\theta + 36 = 0$

$6\cos 3\theta + 12\cos 2\theta + 12 = 0$

Dividing by $6$, we get:

$\cos 3\theta + 2\cos 2\theta + 2 = 0$

Using the multiple angle formulas $\cos 3\theta = 4\cos^3 \theta - 3\cos \theta$ and $\cos 2\theta = 2\cos^2 \theta - 1$, we substitute these into the equation:

$(4\cos^3 \theta - 3\cos \theta) + 2(2\cos^2 \theta - 1) + 2 = 0$

$4\cos^3 \theta + 4\cos^2 \theta - 3\cos \theta = 0$

$\cos \theta (4\cos^2 \theta + 4\cos \theta - 3) = 0$

$\cos \theta (2\cos \theta - 1)(2\cos \theta + 3) = 0$

This gives the possible values for $\cos \theta$:

$\cos \theta = 0 \implies \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$

$\cos \theta = \dfrac{1}{2} \implies \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{3}, \dfrac{5\pi}{3}$

$\cos \theta = -\dfrac{3}{2}$ (Not possible since $\cos \theta \in [-1, 1]$)

The possible values of $\theta \in [0, 2\pi]$ are $\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{3\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{3}, \dfrac{5\pi}{3}$.

Sum of all possible values of $\theta$:

$\sum \theta = \left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} + \dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right) + \left(\dfrac{\pi}{3} + \dfrac{5\pi}{3}\right) = 2\pi + 2\pi = 4\pi$

Answer: $4\pi$

questions.q:
If $f: \mathbf{N} \rightarrow \mathbf{Z}$ is defined by
$f(n) = \begin{vmatrix} n & -1 & -5 \\ -2n^2 & 3(2k+1) & 2k+1 \\ -3n^3 & 3k(2k+1) & 3k(k+2)+1 \end{vmatrix}$, $k \in \mathbf{N}$,
and $\sum_{n=1}^{k} f(n) = 98$, then $k$ is equal to :
questions.solution:
Let $S = \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{k} f(n)$, where
$f(n) = \begin{vmatrix} n & -1 & -5 \\ -2n^2 & 3(2k+1) & 2k+1 \\ -3n^3 & 3k(2k+1) & 3k(k+2)+1 \end{vmatrix}$

Since only the first column depends on $n$, the summation can be taken inside that column:
$S = \begin{vmatrix} \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{k} n & -1 & -5 \\ \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{k} (-2n^2) & 3(2k+1) & 2k+1 \\ \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{k} (-3n^3) & 3k(2k+1) & 3k(k+2)+1 \end{vmatrix}$

Using standard summation formulas:
$\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{k} n = \dfrac{k(k+1)}{2}$
$\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{k} (-2n^2) = -\dfrac{k(k+1)(2k+1)}{3}$
$\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{k} (-3n^3) = -\dfrac{3k^2(k+1)^2}{4}$

Substituting:
$S = \begin{vmatrix} \dfrac{k(k+1)}{2} & -1 & -5 \\ -\dfrac{k(k+1)(2k+1)}{3} & 3(2k+1) & 2k+1 \\ -\dfrac{3k^2(k+1)^2}{4} & 3k(2k+1) & 3k^2+6k+1 \end{vmatrix}$

Taking $\dfrac{k(k+1)}{12}$ common from $C_1$:
$S = \dfrac{k(k+1)}{12} \begin{vmatrix} 6 & -1 & -5 \\ -4(2k+1) & 3(2k+1) & 2k+1 \\ -9k(k+1) & 3k(2k+1) & 3k^2+6k+1 \end{vmatrix}$

Applying $C_1 \to C_1 + C_2 + C_3$:
Row 1: $6 - 1 - 5 = 0$
Row 2: $-8k - 4 + 6k + 3 + 2k + 1 = 0$
Row 3: $-9k^2 - 9k + 6k^2 + 3k + 3k^2 + 6k + 1 = 1$

$S = \dfrac{k(k+1)}{12} \begin{vmatrix} 0 & -1 & -5 \\ 0 & 3(2k+1) & 2k+1 \\ 1 & 3k(2k+1) & 3k^2+6k+1 \end{vmatrix}$

Expanding along $C_1$:
$S = \dfrac{k(k+1)}{12} \cdot 1 \cdot \begin{vmatrix} -1 & -5 \\ 3(2k+1) & 2k+1 \end{vmatrix}$

$S = \dfrac{k(k+1)}{12}\left[(-1)(2k+1) - (-5)(3(2k+1))\right]$

$S = \dfrac{k(k+1)}{12}\left[-(2k+1) + 15(2k+1)\right]$

$S = \dfrac{k(k+1)}{12} \cdot 14(2k+1) = 7 \cdot \dfrac{k(k+1)(2k+1)}{6}$

Note that $\dfrac{k(k+1)(2k+1)}{6} = \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{k} n^2$.

Given $S = 98$:
$7 \cdot \dfrac{k(k+1)(2k+1)}{6} = 98$

$\dfrac{k(k+1)(2k+1)}{6} = 14$

Checking integer values of $k$:
$k = 1$: sum $= 1$
$k = 2$: sum $= 5$
$k = 3$: sum $= 14$

Hence, $k = 3$, and the correct option is $(1)\ 3$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q:
Consider the system of linear equations in $x, y, z$:
$x + 2y + tz = 0$,
$6x + y + 5tz = 0$,
$3x + t^2 y + f(t) z = 0$,
where $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is a differentiable function. If this system has infinitely many solutions for all $t \in \mathbb{R}$, then $f$
questions.solution:
For a homogeneous system of linear equations to have infinitely many solutions, the determinant of its coefficient matrix must be zero.

The coefficient matrix is:
$\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 & t \\ 6 & 1 & 5t \\ 3 & t^2 & f(t) \end{vmatrix}$

Expanding the determinant along the first row, we get:
$\Delta = 1(1 \cdot f(t) - 5t \cdot t^2) - 2(6 \cdot f(t) - 3 \cdot 5t) + t(6 \cdot t^2 - 3 \cdot 1)$

$\Delta = f(t) - 5t^3 - 12f(t) + 30t + 6t^3 - 3t$

$\Delta = -11f(t) + t^3 + 27t$

Since the system has infinitely many solutions for all $t \in \mathbb{R}$, we must have $\Delta = 0$ for all $t \in \mathbb{R}$.

$-11f(t) + t^3 + 27t = 0$

$f(t) = \dfrac{t^3 + 27t}{11}$

To determine the nature of the function $f(t)$, we find its derivative with respect to $t$:

$f'(t) = \dfrac{3t^2 + 27}{11}$

Since $t^2 \ge 0$ for all $t \in \mathbb{R}$, we have $3t^2 + 27 \ge 27 > 0$.

Therefore, $f'(t) > 0$ for all $t \in \mathbb{R}$, which implies that $f(t)$ is a strictly increasing function on $\mathbb{R}$.

Answer: is strictly increasing on $\mathbb{R}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q:
If the system of equations:
$x+y+z=5$
$x+2y+3z=9$
$x+3y+\lambda z=\mu$
has infinitely many solutions, then the value of $\lambda+\mu$ is:
questions.solution:
For the system to have infinitely many solutions, $\Delta = 0$ and $\Delta_x = \Delta_y = \Delta_z = 0$.

$\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 3 & \lambda \end{vmatrix} = 1(2\lambda - 9) - 1(\lambda - 3) + 1(3 - 2)$

$\Delta = 2\lambda - 9 - \lambda + 3 + 1 = \lambda - 5$

Setting $\Delta = 0$ gives $\lambda = 5$.

Now, calculating $\Delta_z$:

$\Delta_z = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 5 \\ 1 & 2 & 9 \\ 1 & 3 & \mu \end{vmatrix} = 1(2\mu - 27) - 1(\mu - 9) + 5(3 - 2)$

$\Delta_z = 2\mu - 27 - \mu + 9 + 5 = \mu - 13$

Setting $\Delta_z = 0$ gives $\mu = 13$.

For $\lambda = 5$ and $\mu = 13$, we can verify that $\Delta_x = 0$ and $\Delta_y = 0$ as well.

Therefore, $\lambda + \mu = 5 + 13 = 18$.

Answer: $18$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q:
If the system of equations
$x + 5y + 6z = 4$,
$2x + 3y + 4z = 7$,
$x + 6y + az = b$
has infinitely many solutions, then the point $(a, b)$ lies on the line
questions.solution:
For the given system of equations to have infinitely many solutions, the determinant of the coefficient matrix must be zero, $\Delta = 0$.

$\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 5 & 6 \\ 2 & 3 & 4 \\ 1 & 6 & a \end{vmatrix} = 0$

Expanding along the first row:

$1(3a - 24) - 5(2a - 4) + 6(12 - 3) = 0$

$3a - 24 - 10a + 20 + 54 = 0$

$-7a + 50 = 0 \Rightarrow a = \dfrac{50}{7}$

For infinitely many solutions, we must also have $\Delta_z = 0$.

$\Delta_z = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 5 & 4 \\ 2 & 3 & 7 \\ 1 & 6 & b \end{vmatrix} = 0$

Expanding along the first row:

$1(3b - 42) - 5(2b - 7) + 4(12 - 3) = 0$

$3b - 42 - 10b + 35 + 36 = 0$

$-7b + 29 = 0 \Rightarrow b = \dfrac{29}{7}$

The point $(a, b)$ is $\left(\dfrac{50}{7}, \dfrac{29}{7}\right)$.

Checking the given options, we evaluate $a - b$:

$a - b = \dfrac{50}{7} - \dfrac{29}{7} = \dfrac{21}{7} = 3$

Therefore, the point $(a, b)$ lies on the line $x - y = 3$.

Answer: $x - y = 3$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q:
Let $\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{R}$ be such that the system of linear equations
$x + 2y + z = 5$
$2x + y + \alpha z = 5$
$8x + 4y + \beta z = 18$
has no solution. Then $\dfrac{\beta}{\alpha}$ is equal to :
questions.solution:
The given system of linear equations is:
$x + 2y + z = 5$
$2x + y + \alpha z = 5$
$8x + 4y + \beta z = 18$

For the system to have no solution, the determinant of the coefficient matrix $D$ must be zero.

$D = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & \alpha \\ 8 & 4 & \beta \end{vmatrix} = 0$

Expanding along the first row:

$1(\beta - 4\alpha) - 2(2\beta - 8\alpha) + 1(8 - 8) = 0$

$\beta - 4\alpha - 4\beta + 16\alpha = 0$

$12\alpha - 3\beta = 0$

$\beta = 4\alpha$

To verify the no solution condition, substitute $\beta = 4\alpha$ into the third equation:

$8x + 4y + 4\alpha z = 18$

$4(2x + y + \alpha z) = 18$

$2x + y + \alpha z = \dfrac{9}{2}$

However, the second equation is $2x + y + \alpha z = 5$. This results in a contradiction since $\dfrac{9}{2} \neq 5$. Thus, the system has no solution when $\beta = 4\alpha$.

Therefore, $\dfrac{\beta}{\alpha} = 4$.

Answer: $4$

For consistency: $b - 6 = 8 \Rightarrow b = 14$.
When $a = 8, b = 14$: the system has infinitely many solutions.

questions.q:
Among the statements :
I: If $\left|\begin{array}{ccc}1 & \cos \alpha & \cos \beta \\ \cos \alpha & 1 & \cos \gamma \\ \cos \beta & \cos \gamma & 1\end{array}\right|=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}0 & \cos \alpha & \cos \beta \\ \cos \alpha & 0 & \cos \gamma \\ \cos \beta & \cos \gamma & 0\end{array}\right|$, then $\cos ^{2} \alpha+\cos ^{2} \beta+\cos ^{2} \gamma=\frac{3}{2}$, and
II : If $\left|\begin{array}{ccc}x^{2}+x & x+1 & x-2 \\ 2 x^{2}+3 x-1 & 3 x & 3 x-3 \\ x^{2}+2 x+3 & 2 x-1 & 2 x-1\end{array}\right|=\mathrm{p} x+\mathrm{q}$, then $\mathrm{p}^{2}=196 \mathrm{q}^{2}$,
questions.solution:
Statement I: Let $D_1 = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & \cos\alpha & \cos\beta \\ \cos\alpha & 1 & \cos\gamma \\ \cos\beta & \cos\gamma & 1 \end{vmatrix} = 1 - \cos^2\alpha - \cos^2\beta - \cos^2\gamma + 2\cos\alpha\cos\beta\cos\gamma$.
$D_2 = \begin{vmatrix} 0 & \cos\alpha & \cos\beta \\ \cos\alpha & 0 & \cos\gamma \\ \cos\beta & \cos\gamma & 0 \end{vmatrix} = 2\cos\alpha\cos\beta\cos\gamma$.
$D_1 = D_2 \Rightarrow 1 - \cos^2\alpha - \cos^2\beta - \cos^2\gamma = 0 \Rightarrow \cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = 1 \neq \frac{3}{2}$. Statement I is false.
Statement II: Evaluate by substituting $x = 0$: determinant $= -12$, so $q = -12$.
At $x = 1$: determinant $= 12$, so $p + q = 12 \Rightarrow p = 24$.
$p^2 = 576$ and $196q^2 = 196 \times 144 = 28224$. Since $p^2 \neq 196q^2$, Statement II is false.
Both statements are false.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q:
Let n be the number obtained on rolling a fair die. If the probability that the system
$x-\mathrm{n} y+z=6$
$x+(\mathrm{n}-2) y+(\mathrm{n}+1) z=8$
$(\mathrm{n}-1) y+z=1$ has a unique solution is $\frac{k}{6}$,
then the sum of $k$ and all possible values of $n$ is :
questions.solution:
The coefficient matrix has determinant $\det(A) = -(n-1)(n-2)$.
The system has a unique solution when $\det(A) eq 0$, which requires $n eq 1$ and $n eq 2$.
For a fair die, $n \in \{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$, so the unique solution occurs for $n \in \{3,4,5,6\}$.
The probability is $ rac{4}{6} = rac{2}{3}$, giving $k = 4$.
The sum of $k$ and all possible values of $n$ where unique solution exists is $4 + (3+4+5+6) = 22$.

If the system of equations
$3 x+y+4 z=3$
$2 x+\alpha y-z=-3$
$x+2 y+z=4$
has no solution, then the value of $\alpha$ is equal to :
questions.solution:
For no solution $\Delta = 0$
$\begin{vmatrix} 3 & 1 & 4 \\ 2 & \alpha & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = 0$
$\Rightarrow 3(\alpha + 2) + 1(-1 - 2) + 4(4 - \alpha) = 0$
$\Rightarrow 19 - \alpha = 0 \Rightarrow \boxed{\alpha = 19}$
& for $\alpha = 19$
$\Delta_x = \begin{vmatrix} 3 & 1 & 4 \\ -3 & 19 & -1 \\ 4 & 2 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = 3(21) + 1(-1) + 4(-82)$
$\neq 0$
$\therefore$ no solution for $\alpha = 19$

has infinitely many solutions, then $\lambda^2+\lambda$ is equal to
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned}
& (\lambda-1) x+(\lambda-4) y+\lambda z=5 \\
& \lambda x+(\lambda-1) y+(\lambda-4) z=7 \\
& (\lambda+1) x+(\lambda+2) y-(\lambda+2) z=9
\end{aligned}$

For infinitely many solutions
$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{D}=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
\lambda-1 & \lambda-4 & \lambda \\
\lambda & \lambda-1 & \lambda-4 \\
\lambda+1 & \lambda+2 & -(\lambda+2)
\end{array}\right|=0 \\
& (\lambda-3)(2 \lambda+1)=0 \\
& \mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{x}}=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
5 & \lambda-4 & \lambda \\
7 & \lambda-1 & \lambda-4 \\
9 & \lambda+2 & -(\lambda+2)
\end{array}$\right|=0 \\
& 2(3-\lambda)(23-2 \lambda)=0 \\
& \lambda=3 \\
& \therefore \lambda^2+\lambda=9+3=12
\end{aligned}

questions.q:
If the system of linear equations :
$\begin{aligned}
& x+y+2 z=6 \\
& 2 x+3 y+\mathrm{a} z=\mathrm{a}+1 \\
& -x-3 y+\mathrm{b} z=2 \mathrm{~b}
\end{aligned}$
where $a, b \in \mathbf{R}$, has infinitely many solutions, then $7 a+3 b$ is equal to :
questions.solution:
The given equations are
$\begin{aligned}
& x+y+2 z=6 \\
& 2 x+3 y+a z=a+1 \\
& -x-3 y+b z=2 b, \text{ where } a, b, \in \mathbf{R}
\end{aligned}$

For infinite many solutions:
$D=D_1=D_2=D_3=0 \begin{aligned}
& \therefore D=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
1 & 1 & 2 \\
2 & 3 & a \\
-1 & -3 & b
\end{array}\right|=2 a+b-6 \\
& D_1=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
6 & 1 & 2 \\
a+1 & 3 & a \\
2 b & -3 & b
\end{array}\right|=12 a+5 b+a b-6 \\
& D_2=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
1 & 6 & 2 \\
2 & a+1 & a \\
-1 & 2 b & b
\end{array}\right|=-4 a-3 b-a b+2 \\
& \text{ and } D_3=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
1 & 1 & 6 \\
2 & 3 & a+1 \\
-1 & -3 & 2 b
\end{array}\right|=2 a+2 b-16
\end{aligned}$
from above relations
$\begin{aligned}
& a=-2, b=10 \\
& \therefore 7 a+3 b=16
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: Consider the matrices : $A=\left[\begin{array}{ll}2 & -5 \\ 3 & m\end{array}\right], B=\left[\begin{array}{l}20 \\ m\end{array}\right]$ and $X=\left[\begin{array}{l}x \\ y\end{array}\right]$. Let the set of all $m$, for which the system of equations $A X=B$ has a negative solution (i.e., $x < 0$ and $y < 0$ ), be the interval $(a, b)$. Then $8 \int_a^b|A| d m$ is equal to_________
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned} & A=\left(\begin{array}{cc}2 & -5 \\ 3 & m\end{array}\right), B=\left(\begin{array}{c}20 \\ m\end{array}\right) \\ & X=\left(\begin{array}{l}x \\ y\end{array}\right) \\ & 2 x-5 y=20 \ldots(1)\\ & 3 x+m y=m \ldots(2)\\ & \Rightarrow y=\frac{2 m-60}{2 m+15} \\ & y < 0 \Rightarrow m \in\left(\frac{-15}{2}, 30\right)\end{aligned}$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{x}=\frac{25 \mathrm{~m}}{2 \mathrm{~m}+15} \\ & \mathrm{x} < 0 \Rightarrow \mathrm{m} \in\left(\frac{-15}{2}, 0\right) \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{m} \in\left(\frac{-15}{2}, 0\right) \\ & |\mathrm{A}|=2 \mathrm{~m}+15 \end{aligned}$
Now, $\begin{aligned} & 8 \int_{\frac{-15}{2}}^0(2 \mathrm{~m}+15) \mathrm{dm}=8\left\{\mathrm{~m}^2+15 \mathrm{~m}\right\}_{\frac{-15}{2}}^0 \\ & \Rightarrow 8\left\{-\left(\frac{225}{4}-\frac{225}{2}\right)\right\} \\ & =8 \times \frac{225}{4}=450 \end{aligned}$

questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \alpha \beta \gamma=45, \alpha \beta \gamma \in \mathrm{R} \\ & \mathrm{x}(\alpha, 1,2)+\mathrm{y}(1, \beta, 2)+\mathrm{z}(2,3, \gamma)=(0,0,0) \\ & \mathrm{x}, \mathrm{y}, \mathrm{z} \in \mathrm{R}, \mathrm{xyz} \neq 0 \\ & \alpha \mathrm{x}+\mathrm{y}+2 \mathrm{z}=0 \\ & \mathrm{x}+\beta \mathrm{y}+3 \mathrm{z}=0 \\ & 2 \mathrm{x}+2 \mathrm{y}+\gamma \mathrm{z}=0 \\ & \mathrm{xyz} \neq 0 \Rightarrow \text{ non-trivial } \\ & \left|\begin{array}{lll}\alpha & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & \beta & 3 \\ 2 & 2 & \gamma\end{array}\right|=0\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \alpha(\beta \gamma-6)-1(\gamma-6)+2(2-2 \beta)=0 \\ & \Rightarrow \alpha \beta \gamma-6 \alpha-\gamma+6+4-4 \beta=0 \\ & \Rightarrow 6 \alpha+4 \beta+\gamma=55\end{aligned}$

questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned}
& 11 x+y+\lambda z=-5 \\
& 2 x+3 y+5 z=3 \\

\end{aligned}$
for infinite sol.
$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{D}=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}

questions.q:
If the system of equations
$\begin{aligned}
& x+(\sqrt{2} \sin \alpha) y+(\sqrt{2} \cos \alpha) z=0 \\
& x+(\cos \alpha) y+(\sin \alpha) z=0 \\
& x+(\sin \alpha) y-(\cos \alpha) z=0
\end{aligned}$
has a non-trivial solution, then $\alpha \in\left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$ is equal to :
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \left|\begin{array}{ccc}1 & \sqrt{2} \sin \alpha & \sqrt{2} \cos \alpha \\ 1 & \sin \alpha & -\cos \alpha \\ 1 & \cos \alpha & \sin \alpha\end{array}\right|=0 \\ & \Rightarrow 1-\sqrt{2} \sin \alpha(\sin \alpha+\cos \alpha)+\sqrt{2} \cos \alpha(\cos \alpha-\sin \alpha)=0 \\ & \Rightarrow 1+\sqrt{2} \cos 2 \alpha-\sqrt{2} \sin 2 \alpha=0 \\ & \cos 2 \alpha-\sin 2 \alpha=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ & \cos \left(2 \alpha+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=-\frac{1}{2} \\ & 2 \alpha+\frac{\pi}{4}=2 \mathrm{n} \pi \pm \frac{2 \pi}{3} \\ & \alpha+\frac{\pi}{8}=\mathrm{n} \pi \pm \frac{\pi}{3} \\ & \mathrm{n}=0 \\ & \mathrm{x}=\frac{\pi}{3}-\frac{\pi}{8}=\frac{5 \pi}{24}\end{aligned}$

questions.q: Let the system of equations $x + 2y + 3z = 5, 2x + 3y + z = 9, 4x + 3y + \lambdaz = \mu$ have infinite number of solutions. Then $\lambda + 2\mu$ is equal to:
questions.solution:
Given: $x + 2y + 3z = 5$, $2x + 3y + z = 9$ and $4x + 3y + \lambdaz = \mu$.

For infinite solutions, $\Delta = {\Delta}_{1} = {\Delta}_{2} = {\Delta}_{3} = 0$.

$⇒ \Delta = \left|\begin{cases}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 4 & 3 & \lambda\end{cases}\right| = 0$

$⇒ 3\lambda - 3 - 4\lambda + 8 + 18 - 36 = 0$

$⇒ \lambda = - 13$

Now, finding 

$⇒ {\Delta}_{1} = \left|\begin{cases}5 & 2 & 3 \\ 9 & 3 & 1 \\ \mu & 3 & - 13\end{cases}\right| = 0$

$⇒ \mu = 15$

Now, finding

$⇒ {\Delta}_{2} = \left|\begin{cases}1 & 5 & 3 \\ 2 & 9 & 1 \\ 4 & \mu & \lambda\end{cases}\right|$

$⇒ {\Delta}_{2} = \left|\begin{cases}1 & 5 & 3 \\ 2 & 9 & 1 \\ 4 & 15 & - 13\end{cases}\right|$

$⇒ {\Delta}_{2} = 0$

And 

$⇒ {\Delta}_{3} = \left|\begin{cases}1 & 2 & 5 \\ 2 & 3 & 9 \\ 4 & 3 & \mu\end{cases}\right|$

$⇒ {\Delta}_{3} = \left|\begin{cases}1 & 2 & 5 \\ 2 & 3 & 9 \\ 4 & 3 & 15\end{cases}\right|$

$⇒ {\Delta}_{3} = 0$

For $\lambda = - 13, \mu = 15$ system of equation has infinite solutions.

$⇒ \lambda + 2\mu = 17$.

questions.q:
If the system of equations

$2x + 3y - z = 5$

$x + \alphay + 3z = - 4$

$3x - y + \betaz = 7$

has infinitely many solutions, then $13\alpha\beta$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Given:

The system of equations,

$2x + 3y - z = 5$

$x + \alphay + 3z = - 4$

$3x - y + \betaz = 7$ have many solutions,

So, $△ = {△}_{1} = {△}_{2} = {△}_{3}$

Now, finding ${△}_{2} = \left|\begin{cases}2 & 5 & - 1 \\ 1 & - 4 & 3 \\ 3 & 7 & \beta\end{cases}\right| = 0$

$⇒ 2\left(- 4\beta - 21\right) - 5\left(\beta - 9\right) - 1\left(7 + 12\right) = 0$

$⇒ 13\beta = - 16$

Now, finding ${△}_{3} = \left|\begin{cases}2 & 3 & 5 \\ 1 & \alpha & - 4 \\ 3 & - 1 & 7\end{cases}\right| = 0$

$⇒ 14\alpha - 8 - 57 - 5 - 15\alpha = 0$

$⇒ \alpha = - 70$

Hence, the value of $13\alpha\beta = 70 \times 16 = 1120$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: Let A be a $3 \times 3$ real matrix such that $A\left(\begin{array}{ll}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{array}\right) = 2\left(\begin{array}{ll}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{array}\right), A\left(\begin{array}{ll}- 1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{array}\right) = 4\left(\begin{array}{ll}- 1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{array}\right), A\left(\begin{array}{ll}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{array}\right) = 2\left(\begin{array}{ll}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{array}\right)$. Then, the system $\left(A - 3I\right)\left(\begin{array}{ll}x \\ y \\ z\end{array}\right) = \left(\begin{array}{ll}1 \\ 2 \\ 3\end{array}\right)$ has
questions.solution:
Let, $A = \left[\begin{cases}{x}_{1} & {y}_{1} & {z}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} & {y}_{2} & {z}_{2} \\ {x}_{3} & {y}_{3} & {z}_{3}\end{cases}\right]$

It is given that, $A\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{ll}2 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{array}\right]$

$⇒ \left[\begin{array}{ll}{x}_{1} + {z}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} + {z}_{2} \\ {x}_{3} + {z}_{3}\end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{ll}2 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{array}\right]$

$⇒ {x}_{1} + {z}_{1} = 2, {x}_{2} + {z}_{2} = 0, {x}_{3} + {z}_{3} = 0 . . . \left(i\right)$

Also, $A\left[\begin{array}{ll}- 1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{ll}- 4 \\ 0 \\ 4\end{array}\right]$

$⇒ \left[\begin{array}{ll}- {x}_{1} + {z}_{1} \\ - {x}_{2} + {z}_{2} \\ - {x}_{3} + {z}_{3}\end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{ll}- 4 \\ 0 \\ 4\end{array}\right]$

$⇒ - {x}_{1} + {z}_{1} = - 4, - {x}_{2} + {z}_{2} = 0, - {x}_{3} + {z}_{3} = 4 . . . \left(ii\right)$

Now, $A\left[\begin{array}{ll}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{ll}0 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{array}\right]$

$⇒ \left[\begin{array}{ll}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{3}\end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{ll}0 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{array}\right]$

$⇒ {y}_{1} = 0, {y}_{2} = 2, {y}_{3} = 0 . . . \left(iii\right)$

Using $\left(i\right)\text{and}\left(ii\right)$,

$⇒ {x}_{1} = 3, {x}_{2} = 0, {x}_{3} = - 1$

$⇒ {z}_{1} = - 1, {z}_{2} = 0, {z}_{3} = 3$

$∴ A = \left[\begin{cases}3 & 0 & - 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ - 1 & 0 & 3\end{cases}\right]$

Now, $\left(A - 3I\right)\left[\begin{array}{ll}x \\ y \\ z\end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{ll}- 1 \\ 2 \\ 3\end{array}\right]$

$⇒ \left[\begin{cases}0 & 0 & - 1 \\ 0 & - 1 & 0 \\ - 1 & 0 & 0\end{cases}\right]\left[\begin{array}{ll}x \\ y \\ z\end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{ll}- 1 \\ 2 \\ 3\end{array}\right]$

$⇒ \left[\begin{array}{ll}- z \\ - y \\ - x\end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{ll}1 \\ 2 \\ 3\end{array}\right]$

$⇒ z = - 1, y = - 2, x = - 3$

$⇒ {x}_{1} + {z}_{1} = 2, {x}_{2} + {z}_{2} = 0, {x}_{3} + {z}_{3} = 0 . . . \left(i\right)$

Also, $A\left[\begin{array}{ll}- 1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{ll}- 4 \\ 0 \\ 4\end{array}\right]$

$⇒ \left[\begin{array}{ll}- {x}_{1} + {z}_{1} \\ - {x}_{2} + {z}_{2} \\ - {x}_{3} + {z}_{3}\end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{ll}- 4 \\ 0 \\ 4\end{array}\right]$

$⇒ - {x}_{1} + {z}_{1} = - 4, - {x}_{2} + {z}_{2} = 0, - {x}_{3} + {z}_{3} = 4 . . . \left(ii\right)$

Now, $A\left[\begin{array}{ll}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{ll}0 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{array}\right]$

Using $\left(i\right)\text{and}\left(ii\right)$,

$⇒ {x}_{1} = 3, {x}_{2} = 0, {x}_{3} = - 1$

questions.q: Consider the system of linear equations $x + y + z = 5, x + 2y + {\lambda}^{2}z = 9$ and $x + 3y + \lambdaz = \mu$, where $\lambda, \mu \in R$. Then, which of the following statement is NOT correct ?
options: System has infinite number of solution if $\lambda = 1$ and $\mu = 13$
System has unique solution if $\lambda \ne 1$ and $\mu \ne 13$
questions.solution:
Given: 

$x + y + z = 5$

$x + 2y + {\lambda}^{2}z = 9$

$x + 3y + \lambdaz = \mu$

$⇒ △ = \left|\begin{cases}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & {\lambda}^{2} \\ 1 & 3 & \lambda\end{cases}\right|$

$⇒ △ = 2\lambda - 3{\lambda}^{2} - \lambda + {\lambda}^{2} + 1$

$⇒ △ = - 2{\lambda}^{2} + \lambda + 1$

We know that for infinite solutions, $△ = 0 \text{ and } {△}_{1} = {△}_{2} = {△}_{3} = 0$

$⇒ - 2{\lambda}^{2} + \lambda + 1 = 0$

$⇒ 2{\lambda}^{2} - \lambda - 1 = 0$

$⇒ \left(\lambda - 1\right)\left(2\lambda + 1\right) = 0$

$⇒ \lambda = 1, \dfrac{- 1}{2}$

Now, finding ${△}_{1}$ for $\lambda = 1$ we get,

${\Delta}_{1} = \left|\begin{cases}5 & 1 & 1 \\ 9 & 2 & 1 \\ \mu & 3 & 1\end{cases}\right|$

$⇒ {\Delta}_{1} = \mu - 13$

And for $\lambda = \dfrac{- 1}{2}$ we get,

${\Delta}_{1} = \left|\begin{cases}5 & 1 & 1 \\ 9 & 2 & \dfrac{1}{4} \\ \mu & 3 & \dfrac{- 1}{2}\end{cases}\right| = \dfrac{1}{4}\left|\begin{cases}5 & 1 & 4 \\ 9 & 2 & 1 \\ \mu & 3 & - 2\end{cases}\right| = \dfrac{7}{4}\left(13 - \mu\right)$

So, for $\lambda \ne 1 \text{ and } \mu \ne 13$ system has no solution,

Hence, option $\left(C\right)$ is the correct answer.

$⇒ f\left(x\right) = \left|\begin{cases}2\cos^{4}x & 2\sin^{4}x & 3 + \sin^{2}2x \\ 3 & 0 & - 3 \\ 0 & 3 & - 3\end{cases}\right|$

options: The system has unique solution if $\lambda \ne \dfrac{1}{2}$ and $\mu \ne 1, 15$
The system is inconsistent if $\lambda = \dfrac{1}{2}$ and $\mu \ne 1$
The system has infinite number of solutions if $\lambda = \dfrac{1}{2}$ and $\mu = 15$
questions.solution:
Given: 

System of linear equations,

$⇒ \Delta = 8{\lambda}^{2} - 6\lambda - 4{\lambda}^{2} + 2\lambda + 1$

$⇒ \Delta = 4{\lambda}^{2} - 4\lambda + 1$

$⇒ \Delta = ( 2\lambda - 1{)}^{2}$

For unique solution, $\Delta e 0$.

$⇒ 2\lambda - 1 e 0$

$⇒ \lambda e \dfrac{1}{2}$

Let, $\Delta = 0, \lambda = \dfrac{1}{2}$

We know that, for infinite solutions, ${\Delta}_{x} = {\Delta}_{y} = {\Delta}_{z} = 0$

$⇒ {\Delta}_{x} = \left| egin{cases}4\mu & 1 & 1 \ 10\mu & 2 & 1 \ {\mu}^{2} + 15 & 3 & 1\end{cases} ight|$

$⇒ {\Delta}_{x} = - 4\mu - 10\mu + {\mu}^{2} + 15 + 30\mu - 2{\mu}^{2} - 30$

$⇒ {\Delta}_{x} = - {\mu}^{2} + 16\mu - 15$

$⇒ ( \mu - 15 ) ( \mu - 1 ) = 0$

So, for infinite solution $\lambda = \dfrac{1}{2}, \mu = 1$ or $15$.

It has infinitely many solutions if $a = 3, b = 8$

System of linear equations,

$x + 2y + 3z = 4$

Now finding,

$△ = \left| egin{cases}2 & 4 & 2a \ 1 & 2 & 3 \ 2 & - 5 & 2\end{cases} ight|$

${△}_{3} = \left| egin{cases}b & 2 & 4 \ 4 & 1 & 2 \ 8 & 2 & - 5\end{cases} ight|$

$⇒ {△}_{3} = 9\left(b - 8 ight)$

questions.q: Let ${D}_{k} = \left|\begin{array}{ll}1 2k 2k - 1 \\ n & {n}^{2} + n + 2 & {n}^{2} \\ n & {n}^{2} + n & {n}^{2} + n + 2\end{array}\right|$. If $\mathop{∑}_{k = 1}^{n}{D}_{k} = 96$, then $n$ is equal to _________.
questions.solution:
Given that ${D}_{k} = \left|\begin{array}{ll}1 2k 2k - 1 \\ n & {n}^{2} + n + 2 & {n}^{2} \\ n & {n}^{2} + n & {n}^{2} + n + 2\end{array}\right|$

$⇒ \mathop{∑}_{k = 1}^{n}{D}_{k} = \left|\begin{cases}∑ 1 & 2 ∑ k & 2 ∑ k - ∑ 1 \\ n & {n}^{2} + n + 2 & {n}^{2} \\ n & {n}^{2} + n & {n}^{2} + n + 2\end{cases}\right|$

$⇒ \mathop{∑}_{k = 1}^{n}{D}_{k} = \left|\begin{cases}n & 2\dfrac{n\left(n + 1\right)}{2} & 2\left(\dfrac{n\left(n + 1\right)}{2}\right) - n \\ n & {n}^{2} + n + 2 & {n}^{2} \\ n & {n}^{2} + n & {n}^{2} + n + 2\end{cases}\right|$

$⇒ \mathop{∑}_{k = 1}^{n}{D}_{k} = \left|\begin{cases}n & n\left(n + 1\right) & {n}^{2} \\ n & {n}^{2} + n + 2 & {n}^{2} \\ n & {n}^{2} + n & {n}^{2} + n + 2\end{cases}\right|$

${R}_{1} \to {R}_{1} - {R}_{2}$ and ${R}_{2} \to {R}_{2} - {R}_{3}$

$⇒ \mathop{∑}_{k = 1}^{n}{D}_{k} = \left|\begin{cases}0 & - 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & - n - 2 \\ n & {n}^{2} + n & {n}^{2} + n + 2\end{cases}\right|$

Expand the determinant along ${R}_{1}$.

$⇒ \mathop{∑}_{k = 1}^{n}{D}_{k} = 2\left(\left(- n\right)\left(- n - 2\right)\right) = 96$

$⇒ {n}^{2} + 2n = 48$

$⇒ n = 6, - 8$

So, $n = 6$

Hence this is the required answer.

If the system of linear equations
$7x + 11y + \alphaz = 13$
$5x + 4y + 7z = \beta$
$175x + 194y + 57z = 361$
has infinitely many solutions, then $\alpha + \beta + 2$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Given,

System of linear equations,

$7x + 11y + \alphaz = 13$
$5x + 4y + 7z = \beta$
$175x + 194y + 57z = 361$

Now we know that, for infinite solution $D = {D}_{1} = {D}_{2} = {D}_{3} = 0$

Now solving $D = 0$ we get,

$\left|\begin{cases}7 & 11 & \alpha \\ 5 & 4 & 7 \\ 175 & 194 & 57\end{cases}\right| = 0$

Now applying operation ${R}_{3} \to {R}_{3} - 25{R}_{1}$ we get,

$\left|\begin{cases}7 & 11 & \alpha \\ 5 & 4 & 7 \\ 0 & - 81 & 57 - 25\alpha\end{cases}\right| = 0$

$⇒ 81 ( 49 - 5\alpha ) + ( 57 - 25\alpha ) ( - 27 ) = 0$

$⇒ 270\alpha = - 2430 ⇒ \alpha = - 9$

And now solving ${D}_{1} = 0$ we get,

$\left|\begin{cases}13 & 11 & - 9 \\ \beta & 4 & 7 \\ 361 & 194 & 57\end{cases}\right| = 0$

$⇒ 13\left(4 \times 57 - 7 \times 194\right) - \beta\left(11 \times 57 + 9 \times 194\right) + 361\left(11 \times 7 + 9 \times 4\right) = 0$

$⇒ 13\left(- 1130\right) - \beta\left(2373\right) + 361\left(113\right) = 0$

$⇒ 13\left(- 10\right) - \beta\left(21\right) + 361 = 0$

$⇒ 21\beta = 231$

$⇒ \beta = 11$

$∴ \alpha + \beta + 2 = 4$

questions.q: If $\left|\begin{cases}x + 1 & x & x \\ x & x + \lambda & x \\ x & x & x + {\lambda}^{2}\end{cases}\right| = \dfrac{9}{8}\left(103x + 81\right), then $\lambda, $\dfrac{\lambda}{3} are$ the roots of the equation
questions.solution:
Given that, $\left|\begin{cases}x + 1 & x & x \\ x & x + \lambda & x \\ x & x & x + {\lambda}^{2}\end{cases}\right| = \dfrac{9}{8}\left(103x + 81\right)$

Put $x = 0$ as $x \in R$

$⇒ \left|\begin{cases}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {\lambda}^{2}\end{cases}\right| = \dfrac{9}{8}\left(103\left(0\right) + 81\right)$

On expanding the determinant we get,

$⇒ {\lambda}^{3} = \dfrac{9}{8} \times 81$

$⇒ {\lambda}^{3} = \dfrac{{9}^{3}}{{2}^{3}}$

$⇒ \lambda = \dfrac{9}{2}$ and $\dfrac{\lambda}{3} = \dfrac{9}{6}$

Now the required quadratic equation is ${x}^{2} - \left(\dfrac{9}{2} + \dfrac{9}{6}\right)x + \dfrac{9}{2} \times \dfrac{9}{6} = 0$

$⇒ {x}^{2} - \left(6\right)x + \dfrac{27}{4} = 0$

$⇒ 4{x}^{2} - 24x + 27 = 0$

Hence, the required quadratic equation is $4{x}^{2} - 24x + 27 = 0$

Let $S$ be the set of values of $\lambda$, for which the system of equations

$6\lambdax - 3y + 3z = 4{\lambda}^{2}$, $2x + 6\lambday + 4z = 1$ and $3x + 2y + 3\lambdaz = \lambda$ has no solution. Then,$12\mathop{∑}_{\lambda \in S}\left|\lambda\right|$ is equal to _______.
questions.solution:
Given,

System of equations,

$6\lambdax - 3y + 3z = 4{\lambda}^{2}$

$2x + 6\lambday + 4z = 1$

$3x + 2y + 3\lambdaz = \lambda$

For no solution $△ = 0$,

So, $\left|\begin{cases}6\lambda & - 3 & 3 \\ 2 & 6\lambda & 4 \\ 3 & 2 & 3\lambda\end{cases}\right| = 0$

$⇒ 9{\lambda}^{3} - 7\lambda - 2 = 0$

$⇒ ( \lambda - 1 ) ( 3\lambda + 1 ) ( 3\lambda + 2 ) = 0$

Hence, $\lambda \in \left\{1, \dfrac{- 1}{3}, \dfrac{- 2}{3}\right\}$

Now putting the value of $\lambda$ in $12\mathop{∑}_{\lambda \in S}\left|\lambda\right|$ we get,

$12\mathop{∑}_{\lambda \in S}\left|\lambda\right| = 12 \times \left(1 + \dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{2}{3}\right) = 24$

$3x + 2y - z = 7$

$4x + 5y + \alphaz = \beta$,

which of the following is NOT correct?
options: The system has infinitely many solutions for $\alpha = – 5$ and $\beta = 9$
The system has infinitely many solutions for $\alpha = - 6$ and $\beta = 9$
The system in inconsistent for $\alpha = – 5$ and $\beta = 8$
The system has a unique solution for $\alpha \ne – 5$ and $\beta = 8$
questions.solution:
Given,

For the system of linear equations

$2x - y + 3z = 5$

$3x + 2y - z = 7$

$4x + 5y + \alphaz = \beta$,

Now finding,

$D = \left|\begin{cases}2 & - 1 & 3 \\ 3 & 2 & - 1 \\ 4 & 5 & \alpha\end{cases}\right|$

$⇒ D = 2\left(2\alpha + 5\right) + \left(3\alpha + 4\right) + 3\left(7\right)$

$⇒ D = 7\alpha + 35$

Now we know that, for unique solution$D \ne 0 ⇒ \alpha \ne – 5$

So, in option $\left(B\right)$\alpha = – 6$ corresponds to infinitely many solution, which is completely wrong hence, this is answer.

questions.solution:
Given,

$S$ be the set of all values of $\theta \in [ - \pi, \pi ]$ for which the system of linear equations
$x + y + \sqrt{3}z = 0$
$- x + ( tan\theta ) y + \sqrt{7}z = 0$
$x + y + ( tan\theta ) z = 0$
has non-trivial solution,

So, by condition of non-trivial solution we get,

$\left|\begin{cases}1 & 1 & \sqrt{3} \\ - 1 & tan\theta & \sqrt{7} \\ 1 & 1 & tan\theta\end{cases}\right| = 0$

$⇒ \left(\tan^{2}\theta - \sqrt{7}\right) - \left(- tan\theta - \sqrt{7}\right) + \sqrt{3}\left(- 1 - tan\theta\right) = 0$

$⇒ \tan^{2}\theta + \left(1 - \sqrt{3}\right)tan\theta - \sqrt{3} = 0$

$⇒ \left(tan\theta + 1\right)\left(tan\theta - \sqrt{3}\right) = 0$

$⇒ tan\theta = \sqrt{3}, - 1$

$⇒ \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{3}, \dfrac{- 2\pi}{3}, \dfrac{- \pi}{4}, \dfrac{3\pi}{4}$

Hence,

$\dfrac{120}{\pi} ∑ \theta = 120\left(\dfrac{1}{3} - \dfrac{2}{3} - \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{3}{4}\right) = 20$

Let $S$ denote the set of all real values of $\lambda$ such that the system of equations

$\lambdax + y + z = 1$

$x + \lambday + z = 1$

$x + y + \lambdaz = 1$
is inconsistent, then $\mathop{∑}_{\lambda \in S}\left({\left|\lambda\right|}^{2} + \left|\lambda\right|\right)$ is equal to
questions.solution:
System of equations

$\lambdax + y + z = 1x + \lambday + z = 1x + y + \lambdaz = 1$

has no solution, so

$\left|\begin{cases}\lambda & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & \lambda & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & \lambda\end{cases}\right| = 0$

$⇒ \left|\begin{cases}\lambda + 2 & 2 + \lambda & 2 + \lambda \\ 1 & \lambda & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & \lambda\end{cases}\right| = 0$

$⇒ \left(2 + \lambda\right)\left|\begin{cases}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & \lambda & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & \lambda\end{cases}\right| = 0$

$⇒ \left(2 + \lambda\right)\left|\begin{cases}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & \lambda - 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & \lambda - 1\end{cases}\right| = 0$

$⇒ \left(2 + \lambda\right){\left(\lambda - 1\right)}^{2} = 0$

$⇒ \lambda = 1, - 2$

For $\lambda = 1$, we get infinite solutions, since equation will be identical.

So,

$\mathop{∑}_{}^{}\left({\left|\lambda\right|}^{2} + \left|\lambda\right|\right) = 4 + 2 = 6$

questions.q: If a point $P\left(\alpha, \beta, \gamma\right)$ satisfying $\left(\begin{cases}\alpha & \beta & \gamma\end{cases}\right)\left(\begin{cases}2 & 10 & 8 \\ 9 & 3 & 8 \\ 8 & 4 & 8\end{cases}\right) = \left(\begin{cases}0 & 0 & 0\end{cases}\right)$ lies on the plane $2x + 4y + 3z = 5$, then $6\alpha + 9\beta + 7\gamma$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Given,

$\left(\begin{cases}\alpha & \beta & \gamma\end{cases}\right)\left(\begin{cases}2 & 10 & 8 \\ 9 & 3 & 8 \\ 8 & 4 & 8\end{cases}\right) = \left(\begin{cases}0 & 0 & 0\end{cases}\right)$

$⇒ \left(\begin{cases}2\alpha + 9\beta + 8\gamma & 10\alpha + 3\beta + 4\gamma & 8\alpha + 8\beta + 8\gamma\end{cases}\right) = \left(\begin{cases}0 & 0 & 0\end{cases}\right)$

Now on comparing both side we get,

$2\alpha + 2\beta + 8\gamma = 0 \ldots \left(1\right)$

$10\alpha + 3\beta + 4\gamma = 0 \ldots \left(2\right)$

$8\alpha + 8\beta + 8\gamma = 0 \ldots \left(3\right)$

Now from $\left(1\right)$ and $\left(3\right)$ by cross multiplication we get,

$\dfrac{\alpha}{1} = \dfrac{\beta}{6} = \dfrac{\gamma}{- 7} = k ⇒ \alpha = k, \beta = 6k, \gamma = - 7k$

Point $P\left(\alpha, \beta, \gamma\right)$ lie on the plane $2x + 4y + 3z = 5 ⇒ 2\alpha + 4\beta + 3\gamma = 5$

$⇒ 2k + 24k - 21k = 5$

$⇒ k = 1$

Hence, $6\alpha + 9\beta + 7\gamma = 6k + 54k - 49k = 11k = 11$.

Let the system of linear equations

$x + y + kz = 2$

$2x + 3y - z = 1$

$3x + 4y + 2z = k$

have infinitely many solutions. Then the system

$\left(k + 1\right)x + \left(2k - 1\right)y = 7$

$\left(2k + 1\right)x + \left|k + 5\right|y = 10$ has :
questions.solution:
Linear equations $x + y + kz = 2$, $2x + 3y - z = 1 and 3x + 4y + 2z = k$ have infinitely many solutions.

Therefore,

$\left|\begin{cases}1 & 1 & k \\ 2 & 3 & - 1 \\ 3 & 4 & 2\end{cases}\right| = 0$

$⇒ 1\left(10\right) - 1\left(7\right) + k\left(- 1\right) = 0$

$⇒ 10 - 7 - k = 0$

$⇒ 3 - k = 0$

$⇒ k = 3$

For $k = 3$, the second system of equations is

$4x + 5y = 7 \ldots \left(1\right)$

$7x + 8y = 10 \ldots \left(2\right)

Clearly, they have a unique solution

Subtracting \left(1\right)\text{$ and }$\left(2\right), we get

$3x + 3y = 3$

$⇒ x + y = 1$

$

questions.solution:
Given,

The system of equations

$x + 2y + 3z = 3 . . . . . . \left(1\right)

$4x + 3y - 4z = 4 . . . . . . . . . $\left(2\right)$

$8x + 4y - \lambdaz = 9 + \mu . . . . . \left(3\right)

Now using$ the $operation, equation \left(1\right) \times 4 - \left(2\right) we get,

$5y + 16z = 8 . . . . . . . . $\left(4\right)$

Now using the operation, equation $\left(2\right)$ \times 2 - $\left(3\right)$ we get,

$2y + \left(\lambda - 8\right)$z = - 1 - \mu . . . . . . . . $\left(5\right)$

Now using the operation, equation $\left(4\right)$ \times 2 - $\left(3\right)$ \times 5$ we get,

\left(72 - 5\lambda\right)z = 21 + 5\mu$

Now given system of equation has infinitely many solutions, so making coefficient of $z$ to be zero and equating $21 + 5\mu$ with zero we get,

$72 - 5\lambda = 0 ⇒ \lambda = \dfrac{72}{5} a$nd $21 + 5\mu = 0 ⇒ \mu =\dfrac{- 21}{5}$

Hence, the ordered pair $\left(\lambda, \mu\right)$ is equal to $\left(\dfrac{72}{5}, \dfrac{- 21}{5}\right)$.

Let $N$ denote the number that turns up when a fair die is rolled. If the probability that the system of equations

$x + y + z = 12x + Ny + 2z = 23x + 3y + Nz = 3$

has unique solution is $\dfrac{k}{6},$ then the sum of value of $k$ and all possible values of $N$ is
questions.solution:
Given equations are

$x + y + z = 12x + Ny + 2z = 23x + 3y + Nz = 3$

So,

$∆ = \left|\begin{cases}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & N & 2 \\ 3 & 3 & N\end{cases}\right|$

Applying ${C}_{2} ↔ {C}_{2} - {C}_{1}$ and ${C}_{3} ↔ {C}_{3} - {C}_{1}$

$⇒ ∆ = \left|\begin{cases}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & N - 2 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & N - 3\end{cases}\right|$

$⇒ ∆ = \left(N - 2\right)\left(N - 3\right)$

For unique solution $∆ \ne 0$, so

$N \ne 2, 3$

Also, $N \in \left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\right\}$ and for unique solution $N$ can take values $\left\{1, 4, 5, 6\right\}$.

$⇒ P$(system has unique solution ) $= \dfrac{4}{6} = \dfrac{k}{6}$

So, $k = 4$

Therefore, required sum is

$= 4 + 1 + 4 + 5 + 6 = 20$

If the system of equations

$x + y + z = 6$

$2x + 5y + \alphaz = \beta$

$x + 2y + 3z = 14$

has infinitely many solutions, then $\alpha + \beta$ is equal to
questions.solution:
$x + y + z = 6 . . . . \left(1\right)$

$2x + 5y + \alphaz = \beta . . . . \left(2\right)$

$x + 2y + 3z = 14 . . . \left(3\right)$

For infinite solution

$\left|\begin{cases}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 5 & \alpha \\ 1 & 2 & 3\end{cases}\right| = 0$

$⇒ \left(15 - 2\alpha\right) - \left(6 - \alpha\right) + \left(4 - 5\right) = 0$

$⇒ 8 - \alpha = 0 ⇒ \alpha = 8$

$⇒ \left(70 - 2\beta\right) - \left(28 - \beta\right) + 6\left(4 - 5\right) = 0$

$⇒ 36 - \beta = 0$

i.e. $\alpha = 8, \beta = 36$

$⇒ \alpha + \beta = 44$

questions.q:
Let $p$ and $p + 2$ be prime numbers and let
$\Delta = \left|\begin{cases}p ! & \left(p + 1\right) ! & \left(p + 2\right) ! \\ \left(p + 1\right) ! & \left(p + 2\right) ! & \left(p + 3\right) ! \\ \left(p + 2\right) ! & \left(p + 3\right) ! & \left(p + 4\right) !\end{cases}\right|$
Then the sum of the maximum values of $\alpha$ and $\beta$, such that ${p}^{\alpha}$ and ${\left(p + 2\right)}^{\beta}$ divide $\Delta$, is _______.
questions.solution:
Given,

$\Delta = \left|\begin{cases}P ! & \left(P + 1\right) ! & \left(P + 2\right) ! \\ \left(P + 1\right) ! & \left(P + 2\right) ! & \left(P + 3\right) ! \\ \left(P + 2\right) ! & \left(P + 3\right) ! & \left(P + 4\right) !\end{cases}\right|$

Now using the factorial concept and taking common terms we get,

$⇒ \Delta = P ! \left(P + 1\right) ! \left(P + 2\right) ! \left|\begin{cases}1 & 1 & 1 \\ P + 1 & P + 2 & P + 3 \\ \left(P + 2\right)\left(P + 1\right) & \left(P + 3\right)\left(P + 2\right) & \left(P + 4\right)\left(P + 3\right)\end{cases}\right|$

Now on solving determinant we get, $\left|\begin{cases}1 & 1 & 1 \\ P + 1 & P + 2 & P + 3 \\ \left(P + 2\right)\left(P + 1\right) & \left(P + 3\right)\left(P + 2\right) & \left(P + 4\right)\left(P + 3\right)\end{cases}\right|$

Using operation ${C}_{1} \to {C}_{1} - {C}_{2} \text{ and } {C}_{2} \to {C}_{2} - {C}_{3}$

$\left|\begin{cases}0 & 0 & 1 \\ - 1 & - 1 & P + 3 \\ - 2P - 4 & - 2P - 6 & \left(P + 4\right)\left(P + 3\right)\end{cases}\right|$

$= 2P + 6 - \left(2P + 4\right) = 2$

Now putting the value of determinant we get,

$⇒ \Delta = 2P ! \left(P + 1\right) ! \left(P + 2\right) !$

$⇒ \Delta = 2{P}^{3}\left(P - 1\right) ! \left(P + 1\right)\left(P - 1\right) ! \left(P + 2\right)\left(P + 1\right)\left(P - 1\right) !$

Which is divisible by ${P}^{\alpha}$ and ${\left(P + 2\right)}^{\beta}$

So, $\alpha = 3, \beta = 1$

questions.q:
If the system of linear equations.

$8x + y + 4z = - 2$

$x + y + z = 0$

$\lambdax - 3y = \mu$

has infinitely many solutions, then the distance of the point $\left(\lambda, \mu, - \dfrac{1}{2}\right)$ from the plane $8x + y + 4z + 2 = 0$ is:
questions.solution:
Given the system of linear equations.

$8x + y + 4z = - 2$

$x + y + z = 0$

$\lambdax - 3y = \mu$

has infinitely many solutions, so

$D = \left|\begin{cases}8 & 1 & 4 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ \lambda & - 3 & 0\end{cases}\right| = 0 ⇒ \lambda = 4$

Also ${D}_{1} = {D}_{2} = {D}_{3} = 0$

${D}_{1} = \left|\begin{cases}- 2 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ \mu & - 3 & 0\end{cases}\right| = 0 ⇒ - 6 - 3\mu = 0$

So $\mu = - 2$

Hence the point will be $\left(4, - 2, - \dfrac{1}{2}\right)$

Now distance of point $\left(4, - 2, - \dfrac{1}{2}\right)$ from plane $8x + y + 4z + 2 = 0$

$= \left|\dfrac{32 - 2 - 2 + 2}{\sqrt{{8}^{2} + {1}^{2} + {4}^{2}}}\right| = \left|\dfrac{30}{9}\right| = \dfrac{10}{3}$

$3x - y + \left({\lambda}^{2} - \left|\lambda\right|\right)z = 16$ has no solutions, is

$x + 3y - z = - 18$

questions.q:
If the system of linear equations

$2x + 3y - z = - 2$

$x + y + z = 4$

$x - y + \left|\lambda\right|z = 4\lambda - 4$ where $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$,

has no solution, then
questions.solution:
If we have three equations in three variables,

${a}_{1}x + {b}_{1}y + {c}_{1}z = {d}_{1}{a}_{2}x + {b}_{2}y + {c}_{2}z = {d}_{2}{a}_{3}x + {b}_{3}y + {c}_{3}z = {d}_{3}$

then $∆ = \left|\begin{cases}{a}_{1} & {b}_{1} & {c}_{1} \\ {a}_{2} & {b}_{2} & {c}_{2} \\ {a}_{3} & {b}_{3} & {c}_{3}\end{cases}\right|$,${∆}_{1} = \left|\begin{cases}{d}_{1} & {b}_{1} & {c}_{1} \\ {d}_{2} & {b}_{2} & {c}_{2} \\ {d}_{3} & {b}_{3} & {c}_{3}\end{cases}\right|$,${∆}_{2} = \left|\begin{cases}{a}_{1} & {d}_{1} & {c}_{1} \\ {a}_{2} & {d}_{2} & {c}_{2} \\ {a}_{3} & {d}_{3} & {c}_{3}\end{cases}\right|$,${∆}_{3} = \left|\begin{cases}{a}_{1} & {b}_{1} & {d}_{1} \\ {a}_{2} & {b}_{2} & {d}_{2} \\ {a}_{3} & {b}_{3} & {d}_{3}\end{cases}\right|$.

If the set of equations do not have a solution then $∆ = 0$ and at least one among ${∆}_{1}, {∆}_{2}, {∆}_{3}$ is not equal to zero.

$∆ = \left|\begin{cases}2 & 3 & - 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & - 1 & \left|\lambda\right|\end{cases}\right| = 0$

$⇒ \left|\lambda\right| = 7 ⇒ \lambda = \pm 7 \ldots \left(1\right)$

Case 1: $\lambda = 7$

The system of equations are

$2x + 3y - z = - 2x + y + z = 4x - y + 7z = 24$

$a\left(2x + 3y - z + 2\right) + b\left(x + y + z - 4\right) = \left(x - y + 7z - 24\right)$

Comparing the coefficients of $x$ and $y$ we get,

$2a + b = 13a + b = - 1 ⇒ a = - 2, b = 5$

For these values of $a$ and $b$, coefficients of $z$ and the constant values are matching. So the set of equations will have infinitely many solutions.

Case 2: $\lambda = - 7$

The system of equations are

$2x + 3y - z = - 2x + y + z = 4x - y - 7z = - 32$

$a\left(2x + 3y - z + 2\right) + b\left(x + y + z - 4\right) = \left(x - y - 7z + 32\right)$

Comparing the coefficients of $x$ and $y$ we get,

$2a + b = 13a + b = - 1 ⇒ a = - 2, b = 5$

For these values of $a$ and $b$, coefficients of $z$ and the constant values are not matching. So the set of equations will have no solutions.

questions.q: Let $f\left(x\right) = \left|\begin{cases}a & - 1 & 0 \\ ax & a & - 1 \\ a{x}^{2} & ax & a\end{cases}\right|, a \in R$. Then the sum of the squares of all the values of a for $2{f}^{'}\left(10\right) - {f}^{'}\left(5\right) + 100 = 0$ is
questions.solution:
Given, $f\left(x\right) = \left|\begin{cases}a & - 1 & 0 \\ ax & a & - 1 \\ a{x}^{2} & ax & a\end{cases}\right|$

$f\left(x\right) = a\left|\begin{cases}1 & - 1 & 0 \\ x & a & - 1 \\ {x}^{2} & ax & a\end{cases}\right|$

$= a\left[1\left({a}^{2} + ax\right) + 1\left(ax + {x}^{2}\right)\right]$

$⇒ f\left(x\right) = a{\left(x + a\right)}^{2}$

Now differentiating the function w.r.t $x$

We get, ${f}^{'}\left(x\right) = 2a\left(x + a\right)$

Given, $2{f}^{'}\left(10\right) - {f}^{'}\left(5\right) + 100 = 0$

$⇒ 2 \times 2a\left(10 + a\right) - 2a\left(5 + a\right) + 100 = 0$

$⇒ 40a + 4{a}^{2} - 10a - 2{a}^{2} + 100 = 0$

$2{a}^{2} + 30a + 100 = 0$

$⇒ {a}^{2} + 15a + 50 = 0$

$\left(a + 10\right)\left(a + 5\right) = 0$

$a = - 10$ or $a = - 5$

Required $= {\left(- 10\right)}^{2} + {\left(- 5\right)}^{2} = 125$

questions.q: Let $A$ be a $3 \times 3$ real matrix such that $A\left(\begin{array}{ll}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{array}\right) = \left(\begin{array}{ll}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{array}\right); A\left(\begin{array}{ll}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{array}\right) = \left(\begin{array}{ll}- 1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{array}\right)$ and $A\left(\begin{array}{ll}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{array}\right) = \left(\begin{array}{ll}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{array}\right)$. If $X = {\left[{x}_{1}{x}_{2}{x}_{3}\right]}^{T}$ and $I$ is an identity matrix of order $3$, then the system $\left(A - 2I\right)X = \left(\begin{array}{ll}4 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{array}\right)$ has
questions.solution:
Let the matrix be $A = \left[\begin{cases}{a}_{1} & {b}_{1} & {c}_{1} \\ {a}_{2} & {b}_{2} & {c}_{2} \\ {a}_{3} & {b}_{3} & {c}_{3}\end{cases}\right]$

Now $A\left[\begin{array}{ll}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{ll}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2} \\ {c}_{3}\end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{ll}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{array}\right]$

$⇒ {c}_{1} = 1, {c}_{2} = 1, {c}_{3} = 2$

questions.q:
Let the system of linear equations
$x + y + az = 2$

$3x + y + z = 4$

$x + 2z = 1$
have a unique solution $\left(x, y, z\right)$. If $\left(\alpha, x\right), \left(y, \alpha\right)$ and $\left(x, - y\right) are collinear points, then the sum of absolute values of all possible values of$\alpha$ is

$
questions.solution:
Given,
$x + y + az = 2$

$3x + y + z = 4$

$x + 2z = 1$
Now finding,

$\Delta = \left|\begin{cases}1 & 1 & \alpha \\ 3 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 2\end{cases}\right| = - \left(\alpha + 3\right)$

${\Delta}_{1} = \left|\begin{cases}2 & 1 & \alpha \\ 4 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 2\end{cases}\right| = - \left(3 + \alpha\right)$

${\Delta}_{2} = \left|\begin{cases}1 & 2 & \alpha \\ 3 & 4 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 2\end{cases}\right| = - \left(\alpha + 3\right)$

${\Delta}_{3} = \left|\begin{cases}1 & 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 1 & 4 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{cases}\right| = 0$

$\alpha \ne - 3, x = \dfrac{{△}_{1}}{△} = 1, y = \dfrac{{△}_{2}}{△} = 1, z = \dfrac{{△}_{3}}{△} = 0,$

Now points $\left(\alpha, 1\right), \left(1, \alpha\right) \text{ and } \left(1, - 1\right)$ are collinear

$\left|\begin{cases}\alpha & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & \alpha & 1 \\ 1 & - 1 & 1\end{cases}\right| = 0$

$⇒ \alpha\left(\alpha + 1\right) - 1\left(1 - 1\right) + 1\left(- 1 - \alpha\right) = 0$

${\alpha}^{2} + \alpha - 1 - \alpha = 0$

$\alpha = \pm 1$

So, $\left|1\right| + \left|- 1\right| = 2$

The number of values of $\alpha$ for which the system of equations
$x + y + z = \alpha$

$\alphax + 2\alphay + 3z = - 1$

$x + 3\alphay + 5z = 4$

is inconsistent, is
questions.solution:
Given linear equations are

$x + y + z = \alpha$

$\alphax + 2\alphay + 3z = - 1$

$x + 3\alphay + 5z = 4$

For this system of linear equations to have inconsistent solution

$D = \left|\begin{cases}1 & 1 & 1 \\ \alpha & 2\alpha & 3 \\ 1 & 3\alpha & 5\end{cases}\right| = 0$

$⇒ {\left(\alpha - 1\right)}^{2} = 0$

$⇒ \alpha = 1$

Now for $\alpha = 1$

${D}_{1} = \left|\begin{cases}1 & 1 & 1 \\ - 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 3 & 5\end{cases}\right|$

$= \left(10 - 9\right) - \left(- 5 - 12\right) + \left(- 3 - 8\right)$

$= 1 + 17 - 11 \ne 0$

Hence, for $\alpha = 1$ the system of equation has inconsistent solution.

questions.q:
If $\alpha + \beta + \gamma = 2\pi,$ then the system of equations

$x + \left(cos\gamma\right)y + \left(cos\beta\right)z = 0$

$\left(cos\gamma\right)x + y + \left(cos\alpha\right)z = 0$

$\left(cos\beta\right)x + \left(cos\alpha\right)y + z = 0$

has :
questions.solution:
Given, $\alpha + \beta + \gamma = 2\pi$

Now, $\Delta = \left|\begin{cases}1 & cos\gamma & cos\beta \\ cos\gamma & 1 & cos\alpha \\ cos\beta & cos\alpha & 1\end{cases}\right|$

By expanding along the first column, we get

$∆ = 1\left(1 - \cos^{2}\alpha\right) - cos\gamma\left(cos\gamma - cos\alpha . cos\beta\right) + cos\beta\left(cos\alpha . cos\gamma - cos\beta\right)$

$∆ = 1 - \cos^{2}\alpha - \cos^{2}\gamma + cos\gamma . cos\alpha . cos\beta + cos\beta . cos\alpha . cos\gamma - \cos^{2}\beta$

$= 1 - \cos^{2}\alpha - \cos^{2}\beta - \cos^{2}\gamma + 2cos\alpha . cos\beta . cos\gamma$

$= \sin^{2}\alpha - \cos^{2}\beta - cos\gamma ( cos\gamma - 2cos\alpha . cos\beta )$

$= - cos ( \alpha + \beta ) . cos ( \alpha - \beta ) - cos\gamma\left[cos\left\{2\pi - ( \alpha + \beta )\right\} - 2cos\alpha . cos\beta\right]$

$= - cos ( 2\pi - \gamma ) cos ( \alpha - \beta ) - cos\gamma\left[cos ( \alpha + \beta ) - 2cos\alpha . cos\beta\right]$

$= - cos ( 2\pi - \gamma ) . cos ( \alpha - \beta ) - cos\gamma\left[cos\alpha . cos\beta - sin\alpha . sin\beta - 2cos\alpha . cos\beta\right]$

$= - cos\gamma . cos ( \alpha - \beta ) + cos\gamma . cos ( \alpha - \beta )$

$= 0$

So, $∆ = 0$

Hence, the system of equations has infinitely many solutions.

questions.q: If ${a}_{r} = cos\dfrac{2r\pi}{9} + isin\dfrac{2r\pi}{9}, r = 1, 2, 3, \ldots , i = \sqrt{- 1}$, then the determinant $\left|\begin{cases}{a}_{1} & {a}_{2} & {a}_{3} \\ {a}_{4} & {a}_{5} & {a}_{6} \\ {a}_{7} & {a}_{8} & {a}_{9}\end{cases}\right|$ is equal to :
questions.solution:
Given that

${a}_{r} = cos\dfrac{2r\pi}{9} + isin\dfrac{2r\pi}{9}, r = 1, 2, 3, \ldots , i = \sqrt{- 1}$

$⇒ {a}_{r} = {e}^{i\dfrac{2r\pi}{9}} - - - - ( I )$

From Euler form ${e}^{i\theta} = cos\theta + isin\theta$

$\left|\begin{cases}{a}_{1} & {a}_{2} & {a}_{3} \\ {a}_{4} & {a}_{5} & {a}_{6} \\ {a}_{7} & {a}_{8} & {a}_{9}\end{cases}\right|$

$= \left|\begin{cases}{e}^{i\dfrac{2\pi}{9}} & {e}^{i\dfrac{4\pi}{9}} & {e}^{i\dfrac{6\pi}{9}} \\ {e}^{i\dfrac{8\pi}{9}} & {e}^{i\dfrac{i10\pi}{9}} & {e}^{i\dfrac{12\pi}{9}} \\ {e}^{i\dfrac{14\pi}{9}} & {e}^{i\dfrac{i16\pi}{9}} & {e}^{i\dfrac{18\pi}{9}}\end{cases}\right|$

Taking ${e}^{i\dfrac{2\pi}{9}}, {e}^{i\dfrac{8\pi}{9}}, {e}^{i\dfrac{14\pi}{9}}$ common form each row

$= {e}^{i\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{9} + \dfrac{8\pi}{9} + \dfrac{14\pi}{9}\right)}\left|\begin{cases}1 & {e}^{i\dfrac{2\pi}{9}} & {e}^{i\dfrac{4\pi}{9}} \\ 1 & {e}^{i\dfrac{2\pi}{9}} & {e}^{i\dfrac{4\pi}{9}} \\ 1 & {e}^{i\dfrac{2\pi}{9}} & {e}^{i\dfrac{4\pi}{9}}\end{cases}\right|$

We know that If two rows are identical the value of determinant will be equal to zero.

$= 0 - - - ( II )$

Now From equation $( I )$

${a}_{1} = {e}^{i\dfrac{2\pi}{9}}, {a}_{9} = {e}^{i ( \dfrac{2 \times 9\pi}{9} )}, {a}_{3} = {e}^{i ( \dfrac{2 \times 3\pi}{9} )}, {a}_{7} = {e}^{i ( \dfrac{2 \times 7\pi}{9} )}$

${a}_{1}{a}_{9} - {a}_{3}{a}_{7} = {e}^{i\left(\dfrac{20\pi}{9}\right)} - {e}^{i\left(\dfrac{20\pi}{9}\right)} = 0 - - - - ( III )$

From equation $( II ) \text{ and } ( III )$

$\left|\begin{cases}{a}_{1} & {a}_{2} & {a}_{3} \\ {a}_{4} & {a}_{5} & {a}_{6} \\ {a}_{7} & {a}_{8} & {a}_{9}\end{cases}\right| = {a}_{1}{a}_{9} - {a}_{3}{a}_{7}$

questions.q:
If the following system of linear equations
$2x + y + z = 5$
$x - y + z = 3$
$x + y + az = b$
has no solution, then :
questions.solution:
Given system of equations

$2x + y + z = 5$
$x - y + z = 3$
$x + y + az = b$
has no solution,

$D = \left|\begin{cases}2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & - 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & a\end{cases}\right| = 0 ⇒ - 2a - 2 - a + 1 + 2 = 0 ⇒ a = \dfrac{1}{3}$

${D}_{1} = \left|\begin{cases}5 & 1 & 1 \\ 3 & - 1 & 1 \\ b & 1 & a\end{cases}\right| = 5\left(- a - 1\right) + - 1\left(3a - b\right) + 1\left(3 + b\right) = - 8a + 2b - 2$

${D}_{2} = \left|\begin{cases}2 & 5 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & b & a\end{cases}\right| = 2\left(3a - b\right) - 5\left(a - 1\right) + 1\left(b - 3\right) = a - b + 3$

${D}_{3} = \left|\begin{cases}2 & 1 & 5 \\ 1 & - 1 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 & b\end{cases}\right| = 2\left(- b - 3\right) - 1\left(b - 3\right) + 5\left(2\right) = 7 - 3b$

For the system to have no solution $⇒ D = 0, {D}_{3} \ne 0$

$∴ a = \dfrac{1}{3}, b \ne \dfrac{7}{3}$.

$D = \left|\begin{cases}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 2 & 5 \\ 9 & 4 & 28 + [ \lambda ]\end{cases}\right|$

questions.q:
If the system of linear equations

$2x + y - z = 3$

$x - y - z = \alpha$

$3x + 3y + \betaz = 3$

has infinitely many solutions, then $\left|\alpha + \beta - \alpha\beta\right|$ is equal to __________.
questions.solution:
Given,

$2x + y - z = 3$

$x - y - z = \alpha$

$3x + 3y + \betaz = 3$

Let $A = \left[\begin{cases}2 & 1 & - 1 \\ 1 & - 1 & - 1 \\ 3 & 3 & \beta\end{cases}\right] \text{ and } B = \left[\begin{array}{ll}3 \\ \alpha \\ 3\end{array}\right]$

For Equation to have infinitely many solutions $\left|A\right| = 0 \text{ and } \left(Adj . A\right) . B = 0$

$\left|A\right| = \left|\begin{cases}2 & 1 & - 1 \\ 1 & - 1 & - 1 \\ 3 & 3 & \beta\end{cases}\right| = 0$

$⇒ - 3\beta - 3 = 0$

$⇒ \beta = - 1$

Now,

Minor of $A = \left[\begin{cases}2\beta + 3 & \beta + 3 & 6 \\ \beta + 3 & 2\beta + 3 & 3 \\ - 2 & - 1 & - 3\end{cases}\right]$

Cofactor of $A = \left[\begin{cases}- \left(2\beta + 3\right) & - \left(\beta + 3\right) & - 6 \\ - \left(\beta + 3\right) & - \left(2\beta + 3\right) & - 3 \\ 2 & 1 & 3\end{cases}\right]$

Adjoint of $A = \left[\begin{cases}- \left(2\beta + 3\right) & - \left(\beta + 3\right) & 2 \\ - \left(\beta + 3\right) & - \left(2\beta + 3\right) & 1 \\ - 6 & - 3 & 3\end{cases}\right]$

Now, $\left(adj . A\right) . B = 0$

$⇒ \left[\begin{cases}- \left(2\beta + 3\right) & - \left(\beta + 3\right) & 2 \\ - \left(\beta + 3\right) & - \left(2\beta + 3\right) & 1 \\ - 6 & - 3 & 3\end{cases}\right]\left[\begin{array}{ll}3 \\ \alpha \\ 3\end{array}\right] = 0$

$\left[\begin{array}{ll}- 6\beta - 9 - \alpha\beta - 3\alpha + 6 \\ - 3\beta - 9 - 2\alpha\beta - 3\alpha + 3 \\ - 18 - 3\alpha + 9\end{array}\right] = 0$

$⇒ - 18 - 3\alpha + 9 = 0$

$⇒ \alpha = - 3$

Therefore,$\left|\alpha + \beta - \alpha\beta\right| = \left|- 3 - 1 - 3\right| = \left|- 7\right| = 7$

questions.q:
Two fair dice are thrown. The numbers on them are taken as $\lambda$ and $\mu,$ and a system of linear equations
$x + y + z = 5$

$x + 2y + 3z = \mu$

$x + 3y + \lambdaz = 1$
is constructed. If $p$ is the probability that the system has a unique solution and $q$ is the probability that the system has no solution, then:
questions.solution:
$\left|\begin{cases}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 3 & \lambda\end{cases}\right| = \lambda - 5$

${\Delta}_{1} = \left|\begin{cases}1 & 1 & 5 \\ 2 & 3 & \mu \\ 3 & \lambda & 1\end{cases}\right| = 10\lambda + 3\mu - \lambda \mu - 44$

${\Delta}_{2} = \left|\begin{cases}1 & 1 & 5 \\ 1 & 3 & \mu \\ 1 & \lambda & 1\end{cases}\right| = 5\lambda + \mu - \lambda \mu - 13$

${\Delta}_{3} = \left|\begin{cases}1 & 1 & 5 \\ 1 & 2 & \mu \\ 1 & 3 & 1\end{cases}\right| = - 2\mu + 6$

For unique solution
$\lambda \ne 5, \mu \in { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 }$

$⇒ p = \dfrac{5}{6} \times 1 = \dfrac{5}{6}$
For No Solution
$\lambda = 5, \mu \ne 3$

$⇒ q = \dfrac{1}{6} \times \dfrac{5}{6} = \dfrac{5}{36}$

questions.q:
Let $\theta \in \left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$. If the system of linear equations
$\left(1 + \cos^{2} ⁡ \theta\right)x + \sin^{2} ⁡ \thetay + 4sin ⁡ 3\thetaz = 0$

$\cos^{2} ⁡ \thetax + \left(1 + \sin^{2} ⁡ \theta\right)y + 4sin ⁡ 3\thetaz = 0$

$\cos^{2} ⁡ \thetax + \sin^{2} ⁡ \thetay + ( 1 + 4sin ⁡ 3\theta ) z = 0$
has a non-trivial solution, then the value of $\theta$ is:
questions.solution:
$\left|\begin{cases}1 + \cos^{2}\theta & \sin^{2}\theta & 4sin3\theta \\ \cos^{2}\theta & 1 + \sin^{2}\theta & 4sin3\theta \\ \cos^{2}\theta & \sin^{2}\theta & 1 + 4sin3\theta\end{cases}\right| = 0$

${R}_{3} \to {R}_{3} - {R}_{2}$

$\left|\begin{cases}1 + \cos^{2}\theta & \sin^{2}\theta & 4sin3\theta \\ \cos^{2}\theta & 1 + \sin^{2}\theta & 4sin3\theta \\ 0 & - 1 & 1\end{cases}\right|$

${C}_{2} \to {C}_{2} + {C}_{1}$

$\left|\begin{cases}1 + \cos^{2}\theta & 2 & 4sin3\theta \\ \cos^{2}\theta & 2 & 4sin3\theta \\ 0 & - 1 & 1\end{cases}\right|$

${C}_{2} \to {C}_{2} + {C}_{3}$

$\left|\begin{cases}1 + \cos^{2}\theta & 2 + 4sin3\theta & 4sin3\theta \\ \cos^{2}\theta & 2 + 4sin3\theta & 4sin3\theta \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{cases}\right| = 0$

Expanding along ${R}_{3}$

$⇒ \left(1 + \cos^{2}\theta\right)\left(2 + 4sin3\theta\right) - \left(2 + 4sin3\theta\right)\left(\cos^{2}\theta\right) = 0$

$⇒ \left(2 + 4sin3\theta\right)\left(1 + \cos^{2}\theta - \cos^{2}\theta\right) = 0$

$⇒ sin3\theta = \dfrac{- 1}{2}$

$⇒ 3\theta = \dfrac{7\pi}{6}$

$⇒ \theta = \dfrac{7\pi}{18}$

questions.q: For real numbers $\alpha$ and $\beta,$ consider the following system of linear equations: $x + y - z = 2, x + 2y + \alphaz = 1$ and $2x - y + z = \beta .$ If the system has infinite solutions, then $\alpha + \beta$ is equal to ______.
questions.solution:
Given system of linear equations are $x + y - z = 2, x + 2y + \alphaz = 1, 2x - y + z = \beta$

Using Cramer Rule, we can say for infinite solutions

$\Delta = {\Delta}_{1} = {\Delta}_{2} = {\Delta}_{3} = 0$

Here, $\Delta = \left|\begin{cases}1 & 1 & - 1 \\ 1 & 2 & \alpha \\ 2 & - 1 & 1\end{cases}\right| = 0$

Apply ${R}_{1} ↔ {R}_{1} + {R}_{3}$

$⇒ \left|\begin{cases}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & \alpha \\ 2 & - 1 & 1\end{cases}\right| = 0$

$⇒ 3\left(2 + \alpha\right) = 0$

$⇒ \alpha = - 2$

And ${\Delta}_{2} = \left|\begin{cases}1 & 2 & - 1 \\ 1 & 1 & - 2 \\ 2 & \beta & 1\end{cases}\right| = 0$

$⇒ 1\left(1 + 2\beta\right) - 2\left(1 + 4\right) - \left(\beta - 2\right) = 0$

$⇒ \beta - 7 = 0$

$⇒ \beta = 7$

$∴ \alpha + \beta = 5$

questions.solution:

questions.q:
The values of $a$ and $b$, for which the system of equations

$2x + 3y + 6z = 8$

$x + 2y + az = 5$

$3x + 5y + 9z = b$

has no solution, are :
questions.solution:
The given equation is

$2x + 3y + 6z = 8$

$x + 2y + az = 5$

$3x + 5y + 9z = b$

So, $D = \left|\begin{cases}2 & 3 & 6 \\ 1 & 2 & a \\ 3 & 5 & 9\end{cases}\right|$

$= 2\left(18 - 5a\right) - 3\left(9 - 3a\right) + 6\left(5 - 6\right)$

$= 36 - 10a - 27 + 9a + 30 - 36$

$= 3 - a$

${D}_{z} = \left|\begin{cases}2 & 3 & 8 \\ 1 & 2 & 5 \\ 3 & 5 & b\end{cases}\right|$

$= 2\left(2b - 10\right) - 3\left(b - 15\right) + 8\left(5 - 6\right)$

$= 4b - 20 - 3b + 15 + 40 - 48$

$= b - 13$

The system of equation has no solution if $D = 0 \text{ and } {D}_{z} \ne 0$

So, If $a = 3, b \ne 13$, then the system of equation has no solution.

questions.q: Let $a, b, c, d$ be in arithmetic progression with common difference $\lambda$. If $\left|\begin{cases}x + a - c & x + b & x + a \\ x - 1 & x + c & x + b \\ x - b + d & x + d & x + c\end{cases}\right| = 2$, then value of ${\lambda}^{2}$ is equal to________.
questions.solution:
Since, $a, b, c \text{$ and } d are in $A . P .$, therefore

$b - a = c - b = d - c = \lambda$

We have,

$\left|\begin{cases}x + a - c & x + b & x + a \\ x - 1 & x + c & x + b \\ x - b + d & x + d & x + c\end{cases}\right| = 2$

${C}_{2} \to {C}_{2} - {C}_{3}$

$⇒ \left|\begin{cases}x - 2\lambda & \lambda & x + a \\ x - 1 & \lambda & x + b \\ x + 2\lambda & \lambda & x + c\end{cases}\right| = 2$

${R}_{2} \to {R}_{2} - {R}_{1}, {R}_{3} \to {R}_{3} - {R}_{1}$

$\left|\begin{cases}x - 2\lambda & \lambda & x + a \\ 2\lambda - 1 & 0 & b - a \\ 4\lambda & 0 & c - a\end{cases}\right| = 2$

$⇒ \lambda\left|\begin{cases}x - 2\lambda & 1 & x + a \\ 2\lambda - 1 & 0 & \lambda \\ 4\lambda & 0 & 2\lambda\end{cases}\right| = 2$

$⇒ - \lambda\left(4{\lambda}^{2} - 4{\lambda}^{2} - 2\lambda\right) = 2$

$⇒ {\lambda}^{2} = 1$

questions.q: Let $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ be the real roots of the equation, ${x}^{3} + a{x}^{2} + bx + c = 0,$ ($a, b, c \in R$ and $a, b \ne 0$). If the system of equations (in, $u, v, w$) given by $\alphau + \betav + \gammaw = 0, \betau + \gammav + \alphaw = 0, \gammau + \alphav + \betaw = 0$ has non-trivial solution, then the value of $\dfrac{{a}^{2}}{b}$ is<gwmw style="display:none;"></gwmw>
questions.solution:
Equation ${x}^{3} + a{x}^{2} + bx + c = 0$ has roots $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$. Therefore,

$\alpha + \beta + \gamma = - a$

$\alpha\beta + \beta\gamma + \gamma\alpha = b$

Since the given system of equations has non-trivial solutions,

we have

$\left|\begin{cases}\alpha & \beta & \gamma \\ \beta & \gamma & \alpha \\ \gamma & \alpha & \beta\end{cases}\right| = 0$

or ${\alpha}^{3} + {\beta}^{3} + {\gamma}^{3} - 3\alpha\beta\gamma = 0$

or $\left(\alpha + \beta + \gamma\right)\left[{\alpha}^{2} + {\beta}^{2} + {\gamma}^{2} - \alpha\beta - \beta\gamma - \gamma\alpha\right] = 0$

or $\left(\alpha + \beta + \gamma\right)\left[{\left(\alpha + \beta + \gamma\right)}^{2} - 3\left(\alpha\beta + \beta\gamma + \gamma\alpha\right)\right] = 0$

$⇒ - a\left[{a}^{2} - 3b\right] = 0$

or ${a}^{2} / b = 3$

questions.solution:
Given $x, y, z$ are in arithmetic progression, hence $2y = x + z,$ also $\left|\begin{cases}3 & 4\sqrt{2} & x \\ 4 & 5\sqrt{2} & y \\ 5 & k & z\end{cases}\right| = 0$

Applying ${R}_{2} \to {R}_{1} + {R}_{3} - 2{R}_{2}$

$⇒ \left|\begin{cases}3 & 4\sqrt{2} & x \\ 0 & k - 6\sqrt{2} & 0 \\ 5 & k & z\end{cases}\right| = 0$

$⇒ 3 ( x + 2d ) - 5x = 0$

$⇒ x = 3d$ (Not possible)

$⇒ k = 6\sqrt{2}$

$⇒ {k}^{2} = 72 .

$

questions.q: The system of equations $kx + y + z = 1, x + ky + z = k$ and $x + y + zk = {k}^{2}$ has no solution if $k$ is equal to:
questions.solution:
$kx + y + z = 1$

$x + ky + z = k$

$x + y + zk = {k}^{2}$

$\Delta = \left|\begin{cases}K & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & K & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & K\end{cases}\right| = K\left({K}^{2} - 1\right) - 1\left(K - 1\right) + 1\left(1 - K\right)$

$= {K}^{3} - K - K + 1 + 1 - K$

$= {K}^{3} - 3K + 2$

$= ( K - 1{)}^{2}\left(K + 2\right)$

For $K = 1$

But for $K = - 2,$ at least one out of ${\Delta}_{1}, {\Delta}_{2}, {\Delta}_{3}$ are not zero

Hence for no solution, $K = - 2$

Expanding w.r.t. ${R}_{1}$

$= - \left(2sin2x - cos2x\right)$

So, $f\left(x\right) = cos2x - 2sin2x$

${f\left(x\right)}_{max} = \sqrt{1 + 4} = \sqrt{5}$

questions.q:
For the system of linear equations:

$x - 2y = 1, x - y + kz = - 2, ky + 4z = 6, k \in R$

Consider the following statements:
(A) The system has unique solution if $k e 2, k e - 2 .$
(B) The system has unique solution if $k = - 2 .$
(C) The system has unique solution if $k = 2 .$
(D) The system has no-solution if $k = 2 .$
(E) The system has infinite number of solutions if $k e - 2 .$

Which of the following statements are correct?
questions.solution:
$D = \left|\begin{cases}1 & - 2 & 0 \\ 1 & - 1 & k \\ 0 & k & 4\end{cases}\right| = 4 - {k}^{2}$

so, $A$ is correct and $B, C, E$ are incorrect. If $k = \pm 2$

${D}_{1} = \left|\begin{cases}1 & - 2 & 0 \\ - 2 & - 1 & 2 \\ 6 & 2 & 4\end{cases}\right| = - 48 \ne 0$

So, no solution if $k = \pm 2$

questions.solution:
For inconsistent system of equation the conditions should be $∆ = 0$ and at least one of the ${∆}_{x}or{∆}_{y}or{∆}_{z}$ should not be equal to zero.

Now,

$\Delta = \left| egin{cases}3 & - 2 & - k \ 2 & - 4 & - 2 \ 1 & 2 & - 1\end{cases} ight| = 0$

$⇒ 24 + 2\left(0 ight) - k\left(8 ight) = 0 ⇒ k = 3$

$2x + \left(3\lambda + 1\right)y + 3\left(\lambda - 1\right)z = 0$,

Has non-zero solutions, is ....... .
questions.solution:
$\left|\begin{cases}\lambda - 1 & 3\lambda + 1 & 2\lambda \\ \lambda - 1 & 4\lambda - 2 & \lambda + 3 \\ 2 & 3\lambda + 1 & 3 ( \lambda - 1 )\end{cases}\right| = 0$

${R}_{2} \to {R}_{2} - {R}_{1}$

${R}_{3} \to {R}_{3} - {R}_{1}$

$\left|\begin{cases}\lambda - 1 & 3\lambda + 1 & 2\lambda \\ 0 & \lambda - 3 & - \lambda + 3 \\ 3 - \lambda & 0 & \lambda - 3\end{cases}\right| = 0$

${C}_{1} \to {C}_{1} + {C}_{3}$

$\left|\begin{cases}3\lambda - 1 & 3\lambda + 1 & 2\lambda \\ 3 - \lambda & \lambda - 3 & 3 - \lambda \\ 0 & 0 & \lambda - 3\end{cases}\right| = 0$

$⇒ {\left(\lambda - 3\right)}^{2}\left[6\lambda\right] = 0 ⇒ \lambda = 0, 3$

questions.q: Let m and M be respectively the minimum and maximum value values of $\left|\begin{cases}\cos^{2}x & 1 + \sin^{2}x & sin2x \\ 1 + \cos^{2}x & \sin^{2}x & sin2x \\ \cos^{2}x & \sin^{2}x & 1 + sin2x\end{cases}\right|$ Then the ordered pair (m, M) is equal to:
questions.solution:
$D = \left|\begin{cases}\cos^{2}x & 1 + \sin^{2}x & sin2x \\ 1 + \cos^{2}x & \sin^{2}x & sin2x \\ \cos^{2}x & \sin^{2}x & 1 + sin2x\end{cases}\right|$

${C}_{1} \to {C}_{1} + {C}_{2}$

$\begin{array}{ll}D = 2 1 + \sin^{2}x sin2x \\ 2 & \sin^{2}x & sin2x \\ 1 & \sin^{2}x & 1 + sin2x\end{array}$

$\begin{array}{ll}{R}_{1} \to {R}_{1} - 2{R}_{3}\text{and}{R}_{2} \to {R}_{2} - 2{R}_{3}\end{array}$

$D = \left|\begin{cases}0 & \cos^{2}x & - ( 2 + sin2x ) \\ 0 & - \sin^{2}x & - ( 2 + sin2x ) \\ 1 & \sin^{2}x & 1 + sin2x\end{cases}\right| ⇒ D = - 2 - sin2x$

As range of $sin2x \in \left[- 1, 1\right]$, thus

$m = - 3, M = - 1$

questions.q: The values of $\lambda$ and $\mu$ for which the system of linear equations $x + y + z = 2$, $x + 2y + 3z = 5$, $x + 3y + \lambdaz = \mu$ has infinitely many solutions, are respectively
questions.solution:
For infinite number of solutions, all determinants $D, {D}_{1}, {D}_{2}\text{and}{D}_{3}$ must be zero and planes represented by these equations should not be parallel. So, we have,

$D = \left|\begin{cases}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 3 & \lambda\end{cases}\right| = 0 ⇒ \lambda = 5$

${D}_{1} = \left|\begin{cases}2 & 1 & 1 \\ 5 & 2 & 3 \\ \mu & 3 & \lambda\end{cases}\right| = 0$

${D}_{2} = \left|\begin{cases}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 5 & 3 \\ 1 & \mu & \lambda\end{cases}\right| = 0$

And ${D}_{3} = \left|\begin{cases}1 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 5 \\ 1 & 3 & \mu\end{cases}\right| = 0 ⇒ \mu = 8$

questions.q: If $a + x = b + y = c + z + 1,$ where $a, b, c, x, y, z$ are non-zero distinct real numbers, then$\left|\begin{cases}x & a + y & x + a \\ y & b + y & y + b \\ z & c + y & z + c\end{cases}\right|$ is equal to :
questions.solution:
Given $x + a = y + b = z + c + 1$

Now $\left|\begin{cases}x & a + y & a + x \\ y & b + y & b + y \\ z & c + y & c + z\end{cases}\right| = \left|\begin{cases}x & a + y & a \\ y & b + y & b \\ z & c + y & c\end{cases}\right|\left({C}_{3} \to {C}_{3} - {C}_{1}\right)$

$= \left|\begin{cases}x & y & a \\ y & y & b \\ z & y & c\end{cases}\right|\left({C}_{2} \to {C}_{2} - {C}_{3}\right)$

$= y\left|\begin{cases}x & 1 & a \\ y & 1 & b \\ z & 1 & c\end{cases}\right|$

${R}_{2} \to {R}_{2} - {R}_{1}$ and ${R}_{3} \to {R}_{3} - {R}_{1}$

$y\left|\begin{cases}x & 1 & a \\ y - x & 0 & b - a \\ z - x & 0 & c - a\end{cases}\right| = y\left|\begin{cases}x & 1 & a \\ a - b & 0 & - ( a - b ) \\ z - x & 0 & c - a\end{cases}\right| = y ( a - b ) \left|\begin{cases}x & 1 & a \\ 1 & 0 & - 1 \\ z - x & 0 & c - a\end{cases}\right| = - y ( a - b ) ( c - a + z - x ) = y ( a - b )$

Given $x + a = y + b = z + c + 1$

$= \left|\begin{cases}x & y & a \\ y & y & b \\ z & y & c\end{cases}\right|\left({C}_{2} \to {C}_{2} - {C}_{3}\right)$

$= y\left|\begin{cases}x & 1 & a \\ y & 1 & b \\ z & 1 & c\end{cases}\right|$

${R}_{2} \to {R}_{2} - {R}_{1}$ and ${R}_{3} \to {R}_{3} - {R}_{1}$

$y\left|\begin{cases}x & 1 & a \\ y - x & 0 & b - a \\ z - x & 0 & c - a\end{cases}\right| = y\left|\begin{cases}x & 1 & a \\ a - b & 0 & - ( a - b ) \\ z - x & 0 & c - a\end{cases}\right| = y ( a - b ) \left|\begin{cases}x & 1 & a \\ 1 & 0 & - 1 \\ z - x & 0 & c - a\end{cases}\right| = - y ( a - b ) ( c - a + z - x ) = y ( a - b )$

questions.q: If the minimum and the maximum values of the function $f: \left[\dfrac{\pi}{4}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right] \to R,$ defined by $f\left(\theta\right) = \left|\begin{cases}- \sin^{2}\theta & - 1 - \sin^{2}\theta & 1 \\ - \cos^{2}\theta & - 1 - \cos^{2}\theta & 1 \\ 12 & 10 & - 2\end{cases}\right|$ are $m$ and $M$respectively, then the ordered pair $( m, M )$ is equal to :
questions.solution:
${C}_{2} \to {C}_{2} - {C}_{1}$

$f\left(\theta\right) = \left|\begin{cases}- \sin^{2}\theta & - 1 & 1 \\ - \cos^{2}\theta & - 1 & 1 \\ 12 & - 2 & - 2\end{cases}\right| = 4\left(\cos^{2}\theta - \sin^{2}\theta\right) = 4\left(cos2\theta\right)$

Since $cos2\theta = \cos^{2}\theta - \sin^{2}\theta$

Again, $\dfrac{\pi}{4} \le \theta \le \dfrac{\pi}{2} ⇒ 2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) \le 2\theta \le 2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$

$⇒ \dfrac{\pi}{2} \le \theta \le \pi$∴ \theta \in \left[\dfrac{\pi}{4}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right] ⇒ 2\theta \in \left[\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right]$ i.e., Second Quadrant.

$⇒ - 1 \le cos2\theta \le 0$

$f\left(\theta\right){}_{max} = M = 0$

$f{\left(\theta\right)}_{min} = m = - 4$

questions.q:
Let $\lambda \in R$. The system of linear equations
$2{x}_{1} - 4{x}_{2} + \lambda{x}_{3} = 1$
${x}_{1} - 6{x}_{2} + {x}_{3} = 2$
$\lambda{x}_{1} - 10{x}_{2} + 4{x}_{3} = 3$
is inconsistent for :
questions.solution:
Here, we will use Cramer's Rule according to which, $D = 0$ and, ${D}_{1} \ne 0$ if the system of linear equations is inconsistent. $D = \left|\begin{cases}2 & - 4 & \lambda \\ 1 & - 6 & 1 \\ \lambda & - 10 & 4\end{cases}\right| = 2\left(- 24 + 10\right) + 4\left(4 - \lambda\right) + \lambda\left(- 10 + 6\lambda\right)$

$= 2\left(3{\lambda}^{2} - 7\lambda - 6\right) = 2\left(\lambda - 3\right)\left(3\lambda + 2\right)$

$D = 0 ⇒ \lambda = 3, - \dfrac{2}{3}$

${D}_{1} = \left|\begin{cases}1 & - 4 & \lambda \\ 2 & - 6 & 1 \\ 3 & - 10 & 4\end{cases}\right| = 1\left(- 24 + 10\right) + 4\left(8 - 3\right) + \lambda\left(- 20 + 18\right) = 2\left(3 - \lambda\right)$

For $\lambda = - \dfrac{2}{3}, {D}_{1} \ne 0$

$= 2\left(3{\lambda}^{2} - 7\lambda - 6\right) = 2\left(\lambda - 3\right)\left(3\lambda + 2\right)$

$D = 0 ⇒ \lambda = 3, - \dfrac{2}{3}$

${D}_{1} = \left|\begin{cases}1 & - 4 & \lambda \\ 2 & - 6 & 1 \\ 3 & - 10 & 4\end{cases}\right| = 1\left(- 24 + 10\right) + 4\left(8 - 3\right) + \lambda\left(- 20 + 18\right) = 2\left(3 - \lambda\right)$

questions.q: Suppose the vectors ${x}_{1}, {x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are the solutions of the system of linear equations, $Ax = b$ when the vector $b$ on the right side is equal to ${b}_{1}, {b}_{2}$ and ${b}_{3}$ respectively. If ${x}_{1} = \left[\begin{array}{ll}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{array}\right], {x}_{2} = \left[\begin{array}{ll}0 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{array}\right], {x}_{3} = \left[\begin{array}{ll}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{array}\right]$; ${b}_{1} = \left[\begin{array}{ll}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{array}\right], {b}_{2} = \left[\begin{array}{ll}0 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{array}\right], {b}_{3} = \left[\begin{array}{ll}0 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{array}\right]$, then the determinant of $A$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Let $A = \left[\begin{cases}{\alpha}_{1} & {\alpha}_{2} & {\alpha}_{3} \\ {\beta}_{1} & {\beta}_{2} & {\beta}_{3} \\ {\gamma}_{1} & {\gamma}_{2} & {\gamma}_{3}\end{cases}\right]$. Now satisfying ${x}_{1}, {x}_{2}, {x}_{3}$ in $Ax = b$
$A{x}_{1} = {b}_{1} ⇒ \left[\begin{cases}{\alpha}_{1} & {\alpha}_{2} & {\alpha}_{3} \\ {\beta}_{1} & {\beta}_{2} & {\beta}_{3} \\ {\gamma}_{1} & {\gamma}_{2} & {\gamma}_{3}\end{cases}\right]\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{ll}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{array}\right]$

$⇒ \left\{\begin{array}{ll}{\alpha}_{1} + {\alpha}_{2} + {\alpha}_{3} = 1 \\ {\beta}_{1} + {\beta}_{2} + {\beta}_{3} = 0 \\ {\gamma}_{1} + {\gamma}_{2} + {\gamma}_{3} = 0\end{array}\right \ldots \left(i\right)$

Now

$A{x}_{2} = {b}_{2} ⇒ \left[\begin{cases}{\alpha}_{1} & {\alpha}_{2} & {\alpha}_{3} \\ {\beta}_{1} & {\beta}_{2} & {\beta}_{3} \\ {\gamma}_{1} & {\gamma}_{2} & {\gamma}_{3}\end{cases}\right]\left[\begin{array}{ll}0 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{ll}0 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{array}\right]$

$⇒ \left\{\begin{array}{ll}2{\alpha}_{2} + {\alpha}_{3} = 0 \\ 2{\beta}_{2} + {\beta}_{3} = 2 \\ 2{\gamma}_{2} + {\gamma}_{3} = 0\end{array}\right \ldots \left(ii\right)$

And satisfying ${x}_{3}$ gives,

${\alpha}_{3} = 0$, ${\beta}_{3} = 0$ and ${\gamma}_{3} = 2$

Now using $\left(i\right)\text{and}\left(ii\right)$

${\alpha}_{2} = 0, {\beta}_{2} = 1, {\gamma}_{2} = - 1$ and ${\alpha}_{1} = 1, {\beta}_{1} = - 1, {\gamma}_{1} = - 1$
Thus, $A = \left[\begin{cases}1 & 0 & 0 \\ - 1 & 1 & 0 \\ - 1 & - 1 & 2\end{cases}\right] ⇒ \left|A\right| = 2$
questions.question: Suppose the vectors ${x}_{1}, {x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are the solutions of the system of linear equations, $Ax = b$ when the vector $b$ on the right side is equal to ${b}_{1}, {b}_{2}$ and ${b}_{3}$ respectively. If ${x}_{1} = \left[\begin{array}{ll}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{array}\right], {x}_{2} = \left[\begin{array}{ll}0 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{array}\right], {x}_{3} = \left[\begin{array}{ll}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{array}\right]$; ${b}_{1} = \left[\begin{array}{ll}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{array}\right], {b}_{2} = \left[\begin{array}{ll}0 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{array}\right], {b}_{3} = \left[\begin{array}{ll}0 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{array}\right]$, then the determinant of $A$ is equal to

Let $A = \left[\begin{cases}{\alpha}_{1} & {\alpha}_{2} & {\alpha}_{3} \\ {\beta}_{1} & {\beta}_{2} & {\beta}_{3} \\ {\gamma}_{1} & {\gamma}_{2} & {\gamma}_{3}\end{cases}\right]$. Now satisfying ${x}_{1}, {x}_{2}, {x}_{3}$ in $Ax = b$
$A{x}_{1} = {b}_{1} ⇒ \left[\begin{cases}{\alpha}_{1} & {\alpha}_{2} & {\alpha}_{3} \\ {\beta}_{1} & {\beta}_{2} & {\beta}_{3} \\ {\gamma}_{1} & {\gamma}_{2} & {\gamma}_{3}\end{cases}\right]\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{ll}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{array}\right]$

$⇒ \left\{\begin{array}{ll}{\alpha}_{1} + {\alpha}_{2} + {\alpha}_{3} = 1 \\ {\beta}_{1} + {\beta}_{2} + {\beta}_{3} = 0 \\ {\gamma}_{1} + {\gamma}_{2} + {\gamma}_{3} = 0\end{array}\right \ldots \left(i\right)$

Now

$A{x}_{2} = {b}_{2} ⇒ \left[\begin{cases}{\alpha}_{1} & {\alpha}_{2} & {\alpha}_{3} \\ {\beta}_{1} & {\beta}_{2} & {\beta}_{3} \\ {\gamma}_{1} & {\gamma}_{2} & {\gamma}_{3}\end{cases}\right]\left[\begin{array}{ll}0 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{ll}0 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{array}\right]$

$⇒ \left\{\begin{array}{ll}2{\alpha}_{2} + {\alpha}_{3} = 0 \\ 2{\beta}_{2} + {\beta}_{3} = 2 \\ 2{\gamma}_{2} + {\gamma}_{3} = 0\end{array}\right \ldots \left(ii\right)$

And satisfying ${x}_{3}$ gives,

${\alpha}_{3} = 0$, ${\beta}_{3} = 0$ and ${\gamma}_{3} = 2$

Now using $\left(i\right)\text{and}\left(ii\right)$

${\alpha}_{2} = 0, {\beta}_{2} = 1, {\gamma}_{2} = - 1$ and ${\alpha}_{1} = 1, {\beta}_{1} = - 1, {\gamma}_{1} = - 1$
Thus, $A = \left[\begin{cases}1 & 0 & 0 \\ - 1 & 1 & 0 \\ - 1 & - 1 & 2\end{cases}\right] ⇒ \left|A\right| = 2$

If the system of equations

$x - 2y + 3z = 9$
$2x + y + z = b$
$x - 7y + az = 24,$ has infinitely many solutions, then $a - b$ is equal to ______
questions.solution:
For infinitely many solutions $D = {D}_{1} = {D}_{2} = {D}_{3} = 0$

$D = \left|\begin{array}{ll}1 - 23 \\ 211 \\ 1 - 7a\end{array}\right| = 0$

$⇒ 1\left(- 2 - 3\right) + 7\left(1 - 6\right) + a\left(1 + 4\right) = 0$

$⇒ - 5 - 35 + 5a = 0$

$⇒ a = 8$

${D}_{1} = \left|\begin{array}{ll}9 - 23 \\ b11 \\ 24 - 7a\end{array}\right| = 0$

$⇒ \left|\begin{array}{ll}9 - 23 \\ b11 \\ 24 - 78\end{array}\right| = 0$

$⇒ - b\left(- 16 + 21\right) + 1\left(72 - 72\right) - 1\left(- 63 + 48\right) = 0$

$⇒ - 5b + 15 = 0$

$⇒ b = 3$

similarly ${D}_{2} = {D}_{3} = 0$ for $a = 8, b = 3$

$∴$a - b = 8 - 3 = 5$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q:
Let $S$ be the set of all integer solutions $\left(x, y, z\right)$ of the system of equations

$x - 2y + 5z = 0$

$- 2x + 4y + z = 0$

$- 7x + 14y + 9z = 0$

such that $15 \le {x}^{2} + {y}^{2} + {z}^{2} \le 150$. Then, the number of elements in the set $S$ is equal to ..........
questions.solution:
$x - 2y + 5z = 0 . . . . . . . . . . . \left(i\right)

$- 2x + 4y + z = 0 . . . . . . . . . . $\left(ii\right)$

$- 7x + 14y + 9z = 0 . . . . . . . . . . \left(iii\right)

Applying $2 \times$ equation \left(i\right) +$equation $\left(ii\right)$, we get

$z = 0$

Putting $z = 0$ in equation $\left(i\right)$, we get

$x = 2y$

Given $15 \le {x}^{2} + {y}^{2} + {z}^{2} \le 150$

$⇒ 15 \le 4{y}^{2} + {y}^{2} \le 150$

$⇒ 3 \le {y}^{2} \le 30$

$⇒ y = \pm 2, \pm 3, \pm 4, \pm 5$

$⇒ 8$ solutions.

questions.q: If $\Delta = \left|\begin{cases}x - 2 & 2x - 3 & 3x - 4 \\ 2x - 3 & 3x - 4 & 4x - 5 \\ 3x - 5 & 5x - 8 & 10x - 17\end{cases}\right| = A{x}^{3} + B{x}^{2} + Cx + D$, then $B + C$  is equal to :
questions.solution:
$\Delta = \left|\begin{cases}x - 2 & 2x - 3 & 3x - 4 \\ 2x - 3 & 3x - 4 & 4x - 5 \\ 3x - 5 & 5x - 8 & 10x - 17\end{cases}\right|$

Applying ${R}_{2} \to {R}_{2} - {R}_{1}$, ${R}_{3} \to {R}_{3} - {R}_{2}$, we get

$\Delta = \left|\begin{cases}x - 2 & 2x - 3 & 3x - 4 \\ x - 1 & x - 1 & x - 1 \\ x - 2 & 2\left(x - 2\right) & 6\left(x - 2\right)\end{cases}\right| = \left(x - 1\right)\left(x - 2\right)\left|\begin{cases}x - 2 & 2x - 3 & 3x - 4 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 6\end{cases}\right|$

$= - 3{x}^{3} + 12{x}^{2} - 15x + 6$

$∴ B + C = 12 - 15 = - 3$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q:
Let $S$ be the set of all $\lambda \in R$ for which the system of linear equations

$2x - y + 2z = 2$

$x - 2y + \lambdaz = - 4$

$x + \lambday + z = 4$

has no solution. Then the set $S$
questions.solution:
For no solution $\Delta = 0$ and at least one of ${\Delta}_{1}, {\Delta}_{2}, {\Delta}_{3}$ is non-zero.
$\Delta = \left|\begin{cases}2 & - 1 & 2 \\ 1 & - 2 & \lambda \\ 1 & \lambda & 1\end{cases}\right| = - \left(\lambda - 1\right)\left(2\lambda + 1\right)$
${\Delta}_{1} = \left|\begin{cases}2 & - 1 & 2 \\ - 4 & - 2 & \lambda \\ 4 & \lambda & 1\end{cases}\right| = - 2\left({\lambda}^{2} + 6\lambda - 4\right)$
$\Delta = 0 ⇒ \lambda = 1, - \dfrac{1}{2}$

And for $\lambda = 1, - \dfrac{1}{2}, {∆}_{1} \ne 0$
Hence, $S = \left\{1, - \dfrac{1}{2}\right\}$

questions.q:
For which of the following ordered pairs $\left(\mu, \delta\right),$ the system of linear equations
$x + 2y + 3z = 1$
$3x + 4y + 5z = \mu$
$4x + 4y + 4z = \delta$
is inconsistent?
questions.solution:
$D = \left|\begin{cases}3 & 4 & 5 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 4 & 4\end{cases}\right|\left({R}_{3} \to {R}_{3} - 2{R}_{1} + 3{R}_{2}\right)$
$= \left|\begin{cases}3 & 4 & 5 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{cases}\right| = 0$
Now, let ${P}_{3} ≡ 4x + 4y + 4z - \delta = 0 .$ If the system has solutions it will have infinite solution, so,${P}_{3} ≡ \alpha{P}_{1} + \beta{P}_{2}$
Hence, $3\alpha + \beta = 4$ and $4\alpha + 2\beta = 4 ⇒ \alpha = 2and\beta = - 2$
So, for infinite solution $2\mu - 2 = \delta$

For system to be inconsistent,

$2\mu \ne \delta + 2$
So, checking option, $( 4, 3 )$ satisfies.

$3x + 2y + \lambdaz = \mu \ldots \left(3\right)

From \left(1\right)\text{$ and }$\left(2\right),
If $z = 0 ⇒ x + y = 6 and x + 2y = 10$, $⇒ y = 4, x = 2$
If $y = 0 ⇒ x + z = 6 and x + 3z = 10$, $⇒ z = 2, x = 4$

So, $3x + 2y + \lambdaz = \mu$, must pass through $( 2,4, 0 ) and ( 4,0, 2 )$.

$6 + 8 = \mu ⇒ \mu = 14$
And $12 + 2\lambda = \mu ⇒ \lambda = 1$

So, $\mu - {\lambda}^{2} = 14 - 1= 13$

$

questions.q: If $[ x ]$ denotes the greatest integer $\le x,$ then the system of linear equations $[ sin\theta ] x + [ - cos\theta ] y = 0$, $[ cot\theta ] x + y = 0$
options: has a unique if $\theta \in \left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)$ and have infinitely many solutions if $\theta \in \left(\pi, \dfrac{7\pi}{6}\right)$
have infinitely many solutions if $\theta \in \left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)$ and has a unique solution if $\theta \in \left(\pi, \dfrac{7\pi}{6}\right)$
questions.solution:
$\left[sin ⁡ \theta\right]x + \left[- cos ⁡ \theta\right]y = 0$ and $\left[cos ⁡ \theta\right]x + y = 0$ for infinite many solution
$\left|\begin{cases}\left[sin ⁡ \theta\right] & \left[- cos ⁡ \theta\right] \\ \left[cot ⁡ \theta\right] & 1\end{cases}\right| = 0$
i.e. $\left[sin\theta\right] = \left[- cos\theta\right]\left[cot\theta\right] . . . \left(i\right)$

$cot\theta \in \left(\sqrt{3}, \infty\right) ⇒ \left[cot\theta\right] \in \left\{2, 3, 4, . . . \infty\right\}$
